According to the arrangement proposed in the commencement of our series, we have now arrived at the second class of causes affecting health and longevity, embracing three divisions, viz:

1. The undue excrtion of particular organs, with or without insufficient exercise of other parts.-2. Unnatural or constrained positions in different employments.-3. Temperature and moisture.

We have already alluded to the evils consequent on undue exercise of the muscular system in general, such as hernia, aueurism of the large vessels, hemorrhages from the lungs and nose, and dilatation of the cavities of the heart: to these may be added, sprains and lacerations of the muscles, injuries of the ligaments and invertebral spaces, &c. Thus, we sometimes see the patella or knee-pan fractured by a violent effort at leaping, and the tendo-achilles ruptured by the same cause; and we have lately known the walls of the heart give way by a sudden exertion of lifting a heavy weight. We, however, witness the evil effects of over exertion of particular organs most strikingly manifested where the other parts of the muscular system suffer from inaction. This may be illustrated by reference to an affection of the vocal organs, so prevalent of late among clergymen. Various causes have been assigned for this disease, (bronchitis) such as the use of anthracite coal, wearing cravats, constrained posture in public prayer, speaking in basements or other damp or ill-ventilated places, reading the funeral service with the head uncovered, &c. &c.; but the chief cause, in our opinion, is exercising the vocal organs disproportionately to the rest of the body. Were the whole system hardened by systematic exercise, we should rarely meet with bronchitis, caused by the ordinary efforts of public speaking. We seldom observe this affection among the itinerant Methodist clergy, whose active habits of life tend to invigorate the corporeal powers; nor was

it known in former days, when clergymen were obliged to devote a portion of their time to the cultivation of the soil. It is by no means strange that the vocal apparatus, the most delicate and irritable structure in the body, should give way under the excessive tasks often laid upon it, when there is a general debility and want of tone in the whole muscular tissue. Thus, seamstresses often lose the use of the right hand and arm, from the too constant use of the needle; but stonecutters, who also use the right arm in a still more laborious employment, rarely meet with the same accident; and the reason is to be found in the different degrees of strength and resistance imparted to the system by the different degrees of exercise. Dr. Copland remarks, that over exertion of the vocal organs produces various morbid affections, such as hæmoptysis, laryngeal phthisis, aphonia, œdema of the glottis, functional, and, subsequently, organic diseases of the heart and large vessels; and lastly, nervous and cerebral affections. He believes, however, that the ill effects from this cause are not so great nor so frequent as some writers have stated, and that much of the mischief is referable rather to the enthusiasm of singers and orators, to the passions which are called up during the exercise of their powers, and to the various dissipations and exposures into which their vocations lead them. Besides orators and public singers, actors, and those who play much on wind instruments, are also subject to diseases of the vocal organs, to pains in the chest, affections of the larynx, oedema of the glottis, pulmonary emphysema, and spitting of blood. It is also a well-known fact that street criers often perish from laryngeal consumption, induced by over exerting the voice. Whenever symptoms of these maladies appear, absolute rest of the vocal organs is indispensable to a cure. Other remedial agents it does not fall within our province to indicate.

The eye-sight is often injured among engravers, printers, watchmakers, embroiderers, and painters, by too intense application to minute objects; and among workers at iron forges and furnaces, by the continued or intense action of light.* *The affections thus induced are amaurosis, cataract, inflammation of retina, iris or capsule of the lens, and short-sightedness, from the increased convexity of the eye, from continued compression by the muscles of the eyeballs.

But the most frequent and important examples of the undue exertion of particular organs, to the neglect of others, occur among students and literary men, in the over working of the brain. The brain, as the material organ of the mind, is subject as regards its exercise, to the same laws as the other organs of the body. It may suffer from inactivity as well as from being over worked; and its functions, the intellectual and moral facultiés, acquire strength only by discipline and exercise. It is a remark of Plutarch, that "should the body sue the mind before' a court of judicature for damages, it would be found that the mind would prove to have been a ruinous tenant to its landlord."

This refers doubtless rather to the influence of the passions and emotions upon the body, than to study and mental application; the former proving far the most injurious. Still, there can be no question but that health is often destroyed and life shortened by intellectual pursuits. This is indeed denied by Dr. Dunglison and some other writers; but daily observation proves that it is a fact. Tissot remarks that the disorders produced by the efforts of the mind fall soonest upon such as are incessantly engaged in the contemplation of the same object. In this case, he adds, there is only one part of the sensorium acted upon, and that is kept always on the stretch; it is not relieved by the action of other parts, and therefore is sooner fatigued and injured. Thus Boerhaave, after a long period of intense study, suffered for six weeks from excitement of the brain bordering on insanity; and even the mind of Sir Isaac Newton was for a considerable time disordered by excessive application, and it is believed he never entirely recovered from the shock. Numerous examples of a similar kind might be given, were it necessary; though we are free to acknowledge that in many of these cases literary pursuits have operated chiefly in a negative manner, by inducing those sedentary habits which in all occupations are so prejudicial to health. Unless there is evident cerebral disorder, we should rather refer such consequences to collateral circumstances than to excitement of the brain. "Men of exalted intellect," says the celebrated Pinel, "perish by their brains, and such is the noble end of those whose genius procures for them that immortality which so many ardently desire." Dr.

James Johnson has remarked, that "a high range of health is probably incompatible with the most vigorous exertion of the mind, and that this last both requires and induces a standard of health somewhat below par. It would not be difficult," he adds, "to show that the majority of those who have left behind them imperishable monuments of their intellectual powers and exertions were people of weak bodily health. Virgil, Horace, Voltaire, Pope, and a thousand others might be quoted in illustration." Dr. Dunglison believes that these are only "coincidences, affording examples of high intellectual attainments and productions, in spite of the bodily infirmities under which those distinguished individuals labored, but by no means showing that they were the consequence of such infirmities. Nothing," he adds, "would seem to be clearer than that full intellectual development requires that the different corporeal functions should be faithfully and regularly executed. It is impossible for the mind to aspire to lofty conceptions, or for the various intellectual faculties to be fully accomplished, unless the body be devoid of suffering. Whatever distracts the mind from its own operations, enfeebles the results; and nothing does this more effectually and unpropitiously than suffering of any kind.

On Sunday evening, a thunderstorm struck London, bringing sudden darkness followed by a heavy downpour, lightning flashes, and loud thunder. Later that night, during this same storm, a fatal accident occurred in Wisbeach when Mrs. Rae and her horse were drowned after the horse bolted into a canal while her husband drove. Subsequently, a thunderstorm in Sittingbourne on Sunday struck a man named Marsh, knocking him down and rendering him totally blind; his carriage also sustained damage.

The sequence of severe weather events continued on Monday. A thunderstorm, more violent than a prior hurricane, passed over Preston on Monday night, starting around 10:45 and continuing past one o'clock. During this storm, the lightning was remarkably frequent and intensely bright, featuring both tremulous white and resplendent blue flashes. About midnight, the Mechanics' Arms Inn in Preston was struck by lightning; this caused a chimney stack to be hurled into the yard, torn off slating, melted gas piping, and subsequent ignition of the gas, leading to a fire that the fire brigade eventually extinguished after an hour's work. Separately, lightning split the large chimney at Mr. Charnley's biscuit manufactory off Moorlane, requiring major rebuilding. In the surrounding areas of Peuwortham, Walton, and Fulwood, the lightning severely damaged fruit and other trees by blowing off or shattering whole branches. Heavy rain fell during the storm, and at 12:50, large hailstones were observed.

Near Preston, another heavy thunderstorm struck Leyland. Initially, the lightning was silent, but by twelve o'clock, loud thunder followed. The vivid, almost continuous lightning illuminated a large area. A little before midnight, the house of Mr. Thos. Hesketh in Leyland-lane suffered extensive damage when the electric fluid struck the chimney at the southern gable, completely demolishing it. The lightning then descended the flue, damaging the bedroom fireplace, blackening gilded frames, and breaking numerous panes of glass across the house, eventually upsetting furniture and breaking crockery.

Meanwhile, a severe thunderstorm raged over St. Helens shortly after eleven o'clock on Monday night for about half an hour. The lightning flashed for some time before the thunder arrived, and dense showers followed. During this storm, the lightning struck the roof of a shed in Messrs. Glover's ropery, setting it ablaze, though internal resources handled the fire. Additionally, in St. Anne's, a man named Thomas Cooney was injured after being struck in a cottage damaged in a previous storm; he lost the use of his legs. In a separate incident in Liverpool-road, lightning entered Mr. Stewart's house through the chimney, causing damage to furniture and a looking-glass in the bedrooms.

Tuesday morning brought its own weather events. A thunderstorm of great severity passed over Lancaster around one o'clock on Tuesday. Torrential rain fell for nearly half an hour, causing several bermes in Stonewell to flood considerably. This storm demolished a high wall adjoining the National School in Leonard-gate by several yards, and a chimney at Beaumont Farm outside the town was struck, causing significant damage and igniting some wall paper, though the occupants remained unharmed.

Across the country, other destructive storms were reported. A violent thunderstorm hit Southampton on Monday evening, characterized by extremely vivid lightning and torrential rain; this event resulted in the death of a boy named Green, the killing of a horse, and damage to a house in Fremantle. In Mayo, a terrible thunderstorm swept over the county Monday night and into Tuesday morning, accompanied by intense lightning and heavy rain. This storm caused the electric fluid to enter a fishmonger's house, knocking his wife senseless, injuring canaries in the next house, and having a baker's watch torn out of his hand. Another violent thunderstorm visited Armagh, causing serious damage to two houses, killing a horse, and rooting up trees, while also partially suspending telegraphic communication.

In other locations, isolated incidents occurred. On Tuesday morning, Beechwood Mains Farmhouse near Edinburgh was destroyed by fire, which was believed to have been caused by lightning knocking down part of the chimney, though the two occupants escaped narrowly. Finally, in Antwerp on Monday night and Tuesday morning, a massive warehouse filled with goods was struck by lightning during a thunderstorm, causing it to ignite and be destroyed, resulting in estimated losses exceeding £80,000, though these were covered by insurance.

The journey began near a mountain gap, which formed a semicircle through which three river branches flowed, with several roads converging toward this opening. While some eastern mountains still held snow, the surrounding peaks were heavily covered in snow. On Tuesday the 15th, after an early breakfast, the group proceeded along the buffaloe road over a low mountain gap toward the head of the eastern Fork of Gallatin's river, where they had camped the previous evening. Six miles later, they reached the crest of the dividing ridge separating the Missouri and Yellowstone waters. Descending this ridge led them to one of the Yellowstone's tributaries, which they followed through open country flanked by high, pine-covered mountains and watered by streams densely packed with beaver dams. After nine miles from the ridge crest, they reached the Yellowstone itself, situated about a mile and a half below its Rocky Mountain source. This location revealed that the connection between the two rivers was both short and easy. From the Missouri's three Forks, the total distance was forty-eight miles, mostly across a level plain; even more directly, from the navigable eastern branch of Gallatin's river to this point on the Yellowstone, the distance was less than eighteen miles, featuring an excellent road over dry, low hills.

The party paused for three hours to rest their horses before continuing along the riverbank via the buffaloe road. Despite having just left a high, snowy peak, the Yellowstone was already a bold, rapid, and deep stream, spanning one hundred and twenty yards. Within the mountains, the river bottom was narrow, but in the valley below, it widened to nearly two miles, occasionally overflowing and nourishing cottonwood, rose-bushes, honeysuckle, rushes, common coarse grass, and rye. These low floodplains were bordered on both sides by dry plains of coarse gravel and sand, which stretched to the mountain base and supported only short grass. The eastern mountains proved rough and rocky, still retaining much snow, and two other high, snow-covered peaks were visible—one heading north fifteen or twenty miles, and the other nearly east—neither possessing timber suitable even for a small canoe. At a distance of nine miles from the mountains, a river descended into the Yellowstone from the northwest, emerging from the snowy slopes beneath a high rocky cliff; this feeder stream was about thirty-five yards wide.

## On the Sublime Echoes of Antiquity: A Contemplation of the Lost Glory of Athens

**By A Devoted Observer of the Classical Ruins**

There are certain edifices, wrested from the deep slumber of the ages, which do not merely invite the gaze, but command the very soul to pause, to surrender itself to a profound and ineffable wonder. Such is the singular majesty that attends the remnants of Ancient Athens. Though the dust of centuries hath settled heavily upon these noble stones, and though much of the grand design—indeed, it may be doubted whether the full measure of the one hundred and twenty-four columns requisite to consummate the vision was ever truly raised to the sky—remains tragically lost to our reckoning, we are privileged, by some divine grace, to stand before those fragments that endure.

To the eye of the modern connoisseur, one might labour to dissect the precise harmony of parts and the perfectitude of proportion that wrought such a beautiful result. Yet, let us confess, for the sake of a truer feeling, that such rigorous analysis proves inadequate. For the true enchantment resides not in the geometry, but in the *sensation* it inspires.

When one beholds those surviving columns, there descends upon the spirit a feeling as novel to the contemplative mind as the sight itself—a transport that resists the neat confines of earthly description. It is a vision that seems to mingle the very realm of Architecture with that of Music. A profound mystery, even to the most earnest soul seeking definition, possessed that sight! It was as if one were beholding not mere stone, but a celestial fabrication, a form rising "Out of the earth a fabric huge Rose like an exhalation, with the sound Of dulcet symphonies and voices sweet, Built like a temple, where pilasters round Were set, and Doric pillars overlaid With golden architrave."

One cannot help but muse upon the genius that conceived such a fusion—a temple not merely erected by mortal hands, but seemingly conjured from the very breath of the Muses!

Alas, the narrative of this magnificence is shadowed by the grim calculus of ruin. The history of its descent into decay is shrouded in the same mists of uncertainty as its initial ascent. Yet, the chronicles do not spare us the mention of the hand of Alaric among those whose passage brought forth its destruction. Such is the cruel caprice of Time, that it allows us to stand in the shadow of a triumph, knowing that the triumphant sound has been silenced by the tramp of barbarian feet.

But though the tempest of oblivion threatens to claim every last grace note of this venerable site, we must press onward. One must persevere, to wrestle with the remnants, to coax some semblance of that former glory from these weathered stones, and to draw forth from them the enduring lesson of human aspiration, however tragically curtailed.

Meantime, I think its disadvantages are exaggerated; but, as this is such matter of taste, I will say no more on this head, though I could. But, again, there is no reason to fear "bother with either garden or stables—one good head-gardener and one good head-coachman (and you wouldn't have bad ones) seem better altogether in comparison with any other arrangements.

In 1811, practices in Sicily, particularly in the dungeons of Verres and Messina, were marked by severe cruelty. Prisoners were sometimes bound with small cords, only to be released when signs of suffering appeared, as executioners feared that death might prevent them from obtaining victims for further torture. The text notes that the Sicilian dungeons of Verres served as a model for the dungeons in Messina during the time of Artali. The Sicilian region was characterized by intense cruelty, likened to a "fury for fury—cruelty for cruelty."

The governance in the region was associated with figures like Manhes and Artali. While Manhes was described as inflexible and calm, Artali was characterized as cruel and furious. One ruler was said to have cured a severe ailment in the country, while the other destroyed the land he governed, turning it into a place associated with revenge. The populace of Messina experienced fear and anxiety, with insecurity pervading all aspects of life. Both those who ordered and those who suffered these cruelties faced severe disapproval.

International reaction was also notable; the English, who were present to defend the people, felt immense shame upon witnessing the massacres. The cries of the people brought this tragedy to the attention of Sir John Stuart, commander of the British forces. He dispatched Lord Forbes, accompanied by surgeons, to inspect the horrific dungeons and attend to the wounded prisoners. The English ministry was aware of these conditions, having received irrefutable evidence, though it is unclear whether they fully appreciated the gravity of the torture. The primary concern for the ministry was the negative opinion (odium) generated against the Sicilian government and against England itself.

This situation weakened the defense of the island. Maintaining control of Sicily was strategically important for the English, not only for the island itself but also due to its proximity to Malta and Naples, allowing for potential defensive or offensive maneuvers between the two. The influence of the Queen was a source of anxiety for the English, as the people largely attributed government measures to her, and their resulting alienation from her tended to alienate them from the English allies as well. Consequently, the English began considering solutions to these problems. The Sicilians, who had previously welcomed the arrival of the court in 1799, had become strongly opposed to it.

## A Shadow Upon the Waves: Mysteries from the Orient

**From the Reports of the Italian Consul at Macao**

The ceaseless expanse of the Pacific, that vast and inscrutable theatre where fortunes are won and lives are lost, occasionally yields up a tale so perplexing, so fraught with human drama, that it compels the deepest contemplation of our nature. It is a morbid morsel, a grim rumour whispered across the globe, which has found its way to our notice—a supposed ‘Coolie Mutiny’ unfolding beneath the distant, inscrutable skies of Japan.

The particulars, furnished by the esteemed Italian Consul at Macao, paint a picture steeped in enigma, a narrative stitched together from fragmentary accounts and the sober observations of consular agents. Imagine, if you will, a vessel, robbed of its very markings, sailing as a phantom upon the waters. On the nineteenth of August past, a ship, stripped bare of its topgallant and topmast—as if wounded by some savage gale—was sighted entering the Barbour of Hakodate. Yet, this spectral craft bore no European soul upon its decks, no distinguishing flag, and no official papers to attest to its legitimate passage. It was a vessel cast adrift from the known order.

The Japanese authorities, ever diligent in their duty, took custody of the derelict, and rightly, they deferred the weighty matter to the jurisdiction of the consuls. There, the peculiar tableau unfolded. Forty-seven Chinese souls were apprehended, and from their very lips issued a staggering declaration: that the Europeans, under the duress of inclement weather, had abandoned their charge, deserting the ship in two separate boats.

A closer inspection soon revealed fragments of truth mingled with suspicion. Contracts, bearing the seal and name of the Italian vessel, the *Providenza*, were found among the arrested men. But the investigation did not cease there. Mr. I3ritzow, the acting Italian agent, took command, and upon a more meticulous scrutiny, discovered a bell, engraved with the inscription 'Bertha, 1836,' alongside disconcerting marks of crimson upon the saloon flooring and certain doorways. The very instruments of navigation and defence were absent; no boats, no cannons, merely a silence punctuated by the memory of violence.

These scattered threads, when drawn together, offer a far more sobering portrait. We learn that the *Providenza*, under the command of Captain Nattini, had recently departed this very port, carrying a complement of twenty-eight Europeans and three hundred and twenty Chinese coolies bound for Callao. The Captain, a man who swore before the Consul to exercise every caution lest his fate mirror the tragedy visited upon another vessel, the *Theresa*, expressed profound apprehension for his men. Yet, the fate of the Captain’s own family, his wife and children, remains secured in Lima, far removed from this maritime peril.

What, then, transpired upon those decks? This is the crux of the matter, the unanswered question that hangs like sea-mist over the horizon. The absence of the requisite lifeboats permits a grim hope—that the Captain and his crew might yet surface, perhaps having secured their safety elsewhere.

But one cannot ignore the melancholy commentary provided by the Consul regarding the very system of indentured passage itself. The practice, so long tolerated—that a ship of these labouring souls should lie becalmed in the coastal roads for months upon end, their captivity visible to the gaze of land yet their liberty denied by the confines of the hull—must surely have provided fertile ground for the gestation of discontent. Such prolonged confinement, even in the sight of shores offering respite, doubtless afforded these unfortunate souls ample opportunity to forge the resolve, the grim determination, to reclaim, upon the boundless high seas, the liberty so cruelly denied to them.

A tale of the sea, it seems, is rarely merely a matter of navigation; it is a profound meditation on bondage, desperation, and the inexorable, sometimes savage, will of the human spirit when pressed to its utmost limit. We await further dispatch, hoping for clarity, yet bracing ourselves for the darker possibilities that these watery crypts may yet reveal.

Without entire assent to any of these theories of prehistoric Greece, we may safely conclude from the evidence: that before the Greek race began its career the Greek lands on both sides of the Ægean were the theater of a considerable civilization, measurably advanced in the arts of war and peace, and trading through Phenicia with Egypt. The prehistoric Greeks, whatever their name, Pelasgians, Carians, Phrygians, Leleges, or Achæans, were, almost without doubt, of the Aryan stock, kinsmen by blood and language of the Romans and of the Celtic and Teutonic races which peopled Western Europe. We are taught that somewhere, perhaps in Central Asia, at some time not known, the original Aryan or Indo-Germanic fountain-head began to send out streams of nations. Those who went south and east occupied India; those who went west settled in Europe. One rill of population, flowing across the Egean or through Thrace, filled the valleys of Hellas and the island fringes of its coast. 3

The position of the Greek peninsula exposed it, as we have already seen, to foreign influences, and indeed we find in the religion of its people and the traditions of their early days much that is Phenician and something that is of Egypt. Phenicia occupied the narrow northern coaststrip of Palestine, hemmed in by Mount Lebanon and the

Mediterranean. Sidon first, and afterward Tyre, its two chief ports, were the earliest commercial cities in the world.

Their people were of Semitic race, closely akin to their neighbors, the Hebrews, and sharing the Hebrew aptitude for trade. They wove and dyed fabrics, worked cunningly in metals, and had made progress in architecture before the year 1300 B. C. For the raw materials of their industries they scoured the sea, the chief objects of their quest being the murex shell-fish, which yielded the Tyrian purple dye, and the metals-gold, silver, copper, tin-fine woods, and ivory. It is claimed that the amber beads of Mycena were brought from the Baltic Sea by Phenician traders, and it is not now disputed that the Sidonian fleets went regularly to the tin-mines of Britain. All along shore from the Pillars of Hercules (Gibraltar) to the Pontus

Euxinus (Black Sea) these indefatigable navigators rowed their long black vessels and founded their trading-posts.

Cyprus, its mountains richly veined with copper, lay at their threshold. The purple-fish which they coveted was most abundant in the sound of Cythera, in the Gulf of

Argolis, and in the Euboean waters. The silver of Sunium and Thasos and the gold of the Thracian mountains were alike attractive. The light-skinned, delicate-featured, finely formed men and women of the coasts and islands fetched high prices in the slave-marts of Assyria and Egypt. The grain of Thessaly, Boeotia, Thrace, and Messenia was needed to fill the mouths of the handicraftsmen of the Phenician cities.

To Cyprus was an easy voyage from Sidon, and thence across to Asia Minor, and up and across the Ægean the

strong-oared ships might slip from cove to cove with almost perfect safety. Disembarking, the traders held fairs, bartering their stuffs and hardware for the produce of the country, and if possible kidnapping a cargo of the natives.

Near the mines and corn lands, on beaches by the musselbeds, and where the shoals of tunny-fish made inshore the Phenicians established more permanent settlements, not attempting to conquer and rule the inland territory, but as trading colonies. On all the Ægean coast-lands such colonies were planted. The new settlers followed strange gods. The simple Pelasgi, worshiping the powers of nature and the Aryan heaven-god, Zeus, were introduced to Astarte and Melcarth, the horrid Syrian gods. In later times, when Aphrodite, the goddess of love and beauty, was a chief divinity of Greece, the myths reported that she had sprung from sea-foam at Cyprus and had first come ashore on Cythera. In these two islands were her oldest Grecian temples, and beneath the graces of her character may sometimes be traced the harsh features of Astarte, the Sidonian goddess of lust. Thus the Greeks owed the coarser features of their Aphrodite-worship to their contact with the East; from the same source Heracles (Hercules), the strong man, citybuilder, dragon-slayer, and civilizing force of Greek mythology, probably derived his origin. His mythical birthplace was Thebes, a Phenician colony, as we shall see, and many of his temples were at points where the Syrian colonists were likely to have raised altars to their Moloch and Melcarth.

DR. G. W. BOOT demonstrated a case of brain abscess. The patient was a mau aged 24 years who fell from a high-chair when nine months old and had a hemorrhage from the right ear, with continuous discharge since that time. He served in the Army for two years.

August 27, 1920, he entered the Presbyterian Hospital with an otitis externa. The abscess was opened and the patient went home the following day. Sep-. tember 4th he returned complaining of headache, dizziness, nausea and vomiting, stiffness of the neck and slight earache. He was slightly delirious and constipated. A spinal puncture revealed a cloudy fluid, with 6250 cells; small diplococcus questionable. The cultures remained sterile after seventy-two hours. He was seen on September 5th and a diagnosis of meningitis secondary to a chronic discharge of the ear was made. A mastoid operation was performed and a large cholesteatomatous mass was found in the left antrum. The tegmen seemed softened; the dura was incised and clear fluid found. The temporosphenoidal lobe was incised and a thin, greyish turbid fluid with broken down brain tissue escaped. A drainage tube was inserted after the sinus had been exposed and found normal; the wound was tamponed.

The patient had a stormy convalescence until September 19; on the 21st, sixteen days after the first operation, a probe was passed up the path of the drainage tube and thick pu. was removed, which contained colon bacilli and pneumococcus on culture.

After that the headache disappeared and patient felt fine and only complained that he could not go home.

On September 26th he was permitted to go home as there was no longer any drainage and the wound was granulating nicely.

The temperature before the operation was 101.8° f., at operation 100°, and most of the time was subnormal up to the time of the drainage.

The case was presented at this time because the otologists are divided as to the advisibility of operating on these cases. One group said one should not operate on meningitis, another said not to operate on a brain abscess in the initiatory stage or in the .crminal stage. This patient in the beginning stage of brain abscess had been operated. Dr. Boot had repeatedly operated on patients in that stage and they recovered. He felt sure the attitude taken by the men at the Mayo clinic was wrong-just like the men who said not to operate on an appendix until there was a well walled off abscess. He has now operated upon eight temporo-sphenoidal abscesses and had four recoveries, and had operated on three cerebellar abscesses, with one recovery.

While we write, the President's Annual Message to both Houses of Congress reaches us, and we read it with eagerness. We cannot say much in its favor, and it does not comport with our duty to the Chief Magistrate_of_the Union in the present critical juncture of our national affairs to say much against it. Mr. Lincoln, in part, for the moment, represents the nation, and we cannot well stand by the nation without standing by him; certainly not, till it is clear that he is, through incompetency or some other reason, on the eve of betraying it. We believe him patriotic, conscientious, and anxious to do the best for the country in his power, and, although we regard his policy as far less bold and determined than that the danger that threatens us demands, we remember that he is placed by his countrymen in a position which for him is and must be one of great embarrassment,-of great difficulty and delicacy, and we are disposed to give to all his words and actions the best possible construction, and to make the most liberal allowance for what may seem to us low, narrow, defective, or tame in his mode of conducting the war for the preservation of our national existence. We are loyal to the nation, and will be loyal to the Administration, so long as it shall be loyal to itself.

The Message is comparatively short, and, though it can lay claim to no grammatical purity, or literary elegance, it is a plain, sensible, business-like document, not much above, nor much below what we expected. We believe the

President is disposed to save the Union, but, in our judgment, he has no adequate conception of the conditions on which, and on which alone, it can be done. He is timid where we should wish him to be fearless, and fearless where we should be willing he should be timid. He is bold enough before loyal men, timid almost to shrinking before disloyal men. He is afraid to touch with his little finger thedivine" institution of slavery; but has no fear of sacrificing any number of freemen and any amount of national treasure, to prevent a hair of its head from being singed. He would seem to regard it as a more imperative duty to keep the Border Slave States nominally in the Union, than to suppress the armed rebellion against it.

We fear that he has not emancipated himself from the old slavery domination, or risen above the old notion that the government must be administered in the exclusive interest and according to the wishes of Southern slaveholders. Initially, the author reflects on the necessity of local guides, viewing them as generally "necessary evils," though acknowledging that personal resourcefulness can yield superior knowledge. However, the author concedes that in a time-constrained environment like Rome, a guide becomes nearly indispensable for efficiently navigating and grouping various sites. For this purpose, the author employed Dominique Bartolotti, an acquaintance through the hotel. Bartolotti, despite having a peculiar mix of English, Italian, and French in his speech, proved invaluable because he possessed honesty, a knack for navigating difficult situations—like gaining entry to closed or late-hour locations—and a genuine disposition.

Following their arrangement with Bartolotti, the itinerary began not with the expected major landmark, St. Peter's, but with the Capitoline Hill, a decision Bartolotti strongly advocated for. This initial step was strategically sound because ascending the tower provided the visitors with a foundational, comprehensive map of the city and its points of interest.

From this vantage point, the author gained a broad overview of the surrounding landscape. The view encompassed the Campagna outside the city, featuring the Via Appia and the Claudian Aqueduct, all bordered by scenic mountains. Below this, the Tiber River flowed, separating the ancient ruins that once defined Rome from the contemporary palaces and dwellings of the city. The author noted the profound historical significance of the Capitoline Hill itself, which stands symbolically between the Popes' and Caesars' eras.

While the Capotoline Hill is currently occupied by three Michael Angelo-designed palaces, the focus soon turned to the artistic treasures within. The author dedicated time to examining these collections. Of particular note was the Dying Gladiator, considered a masterpiece of Roman sculpture, whose enduring artistic quality transcends the damage inflicted by centuries. Equally examined was the Marble Faun, though the author admitted a personal lack of preference for the piece despite its renown.

Having observed the sculptures, the group moved on to view the heads of the old emperors, which offered phrenologists a wide array of cranial and physiognomic examples, ranging from Augustus's refined features to Nero's grotesque ones. Subsequently, the visitors paused at the Hall of Bronzes. Here, the effects of time were more severe than with the marble, with rusted and battered vestiges of great works remaining.

Though the author decided against entering the Senator and Conservators' palaces due to the limited time available, a glimpse beneath revealed significant ancient foundations, such as massive, precisely laid blocks of volcanic tufa from the Consular period. The day's activities concluded with a final observation from the Capitol, looking down upon the Tarpéan rock. This entire sequence—from the guide's initial introduction to the strategic ascent of the Capitoline and the subsequent detailed study of art and ruins—demonstrated a logical progression designed to systematically map and appreciate Rome’s layers of history, beginning with a broad overview before delving into specific, impactful details.

A performance featuring singers from the Steppes captivated the audience, presenting a spectacle that was both novel and engaging. The initial procession, comprising men and women entering from opposite sides, possessed a brilliant quality akin to a Carnival parade, yet it was clearly a highly arranged tableau, demonstrating meticulous artistic planning. The leader of the men’s chorus was strikingly dressed in historical Russian attire, featuring a rich, moss-green velvet tunic with gold embroidery, high red morocco boots, and a crimson satin mantle lined with fur. He projected an air of command, entirely absorbed in the musical task at hand. The accompanying singers wore long, double-sleeved tunics of bright blue or crimson, belted at the waist, paired with black leather boots and beaver caps. These performers, drawn from the Cossack and Kalmuck races, presented a visual contrast to the conductor, who appeared suited to Parisian society.

In contrast, the procession of singing girls, led by Zenia, was equally dramatic. Zenia was dressed in an elaborate, fairy-like costume, featuring a lofty, pearl-embroidered headdress resembling a tiara, a pale yellow satin gown veiled with lace, and a stomacher heavily adorned with pearls. Her companions wore simpler, but equally delicate, pink and blue dresses. The overall aesthetic of the female contingent was one of lighthearted fantasy, contrasting with the more "barbaric sombreness" of the men's attire. The performance also included young children, dressed elaborately, who were part of the choir.

The audience initially reacted with skepticism, expecting a performance standard comparable to previously seen Annamite opera or Javanese ballet. However, the vocal performance proved exceptional. The singers achieved a harmony of "seraphic sweetness and consummate musical training," which captivated the audience despite the apparent artlessness of the presentation. The vocal quality was described as possessing "unimaginable sweetness of timbre and faultless unison."

During the intermission, Zenia communicated with Teddie, a member of the chorus. A tenor approached Teddie and handed him a note from Zenia, inviting him to a supper at the railway station before traveling to Nîmes.

The program evolved from light, teasing, and impish songs, suggestive of northern life, to a second part characterized by profound melancholy. This second section included a farewell song of soldiers to their homeland. This piece reached a peak of emotional intensity, moving through patriotic fervor, wistful remembrance, and finally, a heartbroken adieu. As the band marched away, the song faded, leaving the soaring voices of Zenia and her messenger as the final, deeply felt notes. This climactic vocal exchange, conveying a lover's pledge, elicited a powerful and unified response from the audience. The overall achievement was recognized as being significantly more than a mere musical display, demonstrating a profound appreciation for vocal capability and the power of human emotion in art. Following the performance, Teddie felt a shift, recognizing that Zenia seemed to belong to a different social sphere.

Commission. The well had made a crater which was two hundred and twenty-five feet in diameter and fifty feet deep. The Commission and the companies operating in the district shared the expense of having a counter well bored nearby. This well was filled under high pressure with water and mud. When the gas stratum was reached, the mud acted as a valve which effectually shut off the flow of gas into the well which was burning.

It is now more than two years since the war has been actively carried on in this part of Flanders. Both adversaries, convinced of the difficulty of operations on a large scale, have stood on the defensive, each side contenting itself with harassing the forces opposite, and keeping them on the alert by patrolling excursions into No

Abandoning their attempts where nature, apparently so mild, is in reality so stubbornly opposed to invasion, the Allied commanders have decided that it was better worth while to bring the weight of their military effort to bear farther to the south, in a more practicable region-Artois.

As soon as we come to the little rise which limits the plain of the Lys the scenery changes suddenly. The dense

Flemish vegetation which covered the ground stops at the foot of the long ridges whose gentle slopes rise slowly toward the south. This disappearance of trees and meadows, taking place so quickly, means that we are now in a dry country. Even the streams disappear from the surface of the ground. The transformation is due to the chalk rock which forms, in Artois and in Picardy, the basis of the soil. The country also becomes less flat. Only a few kilometres from the lowest point of the hollow of the Lys the altitude is already three hundred feet, and it remains at about that figure until we reach the little hills of the Ile de France.

In marked contrast to Flanders, a flat country with scattered hillocks, a heavy soil forever watersoaked, and a strong growth of trees and plants, the regions which adjoin it on its southern front are table-lands, with a dry soil and a growth which although comparatively scanty is yet fertile, because the brown top-soil which covers the chalk makes much richer loam than the thick Flemish clay. It is evident that an army will find admirable fighting-ground on these great stretches of dry earth, where there is nothing in the way of the view, where vegetation is comparatively sparse, and where the roads are good and numerous. As a result of more favorable conditions the fighting has been violent in this district ever since the end of September, 1914; the Allies have made many powerful offensive attacks, and the battle of Artois is raging there now.

This determination of the combatants not only shows that the region lends itself readily to military operations; it is also a proof of the strategic importance of Artois. On account of its heights, of which we shall speak more at length, this country commands a very wide view. It dominates Flanders; it also dominates

Picardy. In the east a sort of peninsula of dry soil which juts out in the direction of Douai makes it easy to march toward the plains of the Scarpe and the Escaut, and to turn the positions of Lille and Cambrai. Moreover, we have here a great industrial region; the coal-mines of the Pas de Calais, whose possession by the Germans has been such a calamity to France. For all these reasons it is absolutely necessary that the Allies should win and hold the heights of Artois, at whatever cost. The fighting here has been very severe; whether in the north, on the platform of the Gohelle, which falls away toward the plain of the Lys; or in the centre, to gain the ridge of Vimy; or on the way to Arras toward the south, on the hills through which the valley of the Scarpe runs. To the north the ground rises, gradually at first, in an inclined plane to the southward, above the depression of the Lys, up to the ridge of Vimy.

Condé found this highland of the Gohelle, where the chalk is almost on the surface, a battle-field to his taste when he conquered the Archduke Leopold of Austria near Lens, in 1648. The soil was so poor that there was but little cultivation in his day, and the villages were small and widely scattered; there was nothing to impede the free handling of troops. In the nineteenth century, however, the prolongation of the great cannel coalfields was found to lie under that barren plain, and now the largest and richest coal-mines of France are there. A new industrial life has grown up alongside of and in addition to the old, changing the landscape strangely. We see at first the buildings intended to serve the mines: machine-shops and sheds for screening the coal; high brick chimneys for the great pumps; and everywhere the metal towers in which the wheels lowering and lifting the cages of the shafts work silently. Close to these are the pit-dumps; odd little cones about a hundred feet high, the rubbish from the mines-these are the hills of the "black country." Across the plain rolls a flood of one-story houses, built of red brick soon blackened by the smoke which hangs low above them. In them the miners and workmen live; sometimes these new houses seem to smother the old villages with the weight of their red roofs; sometimes they add to the old crooked streets new ones laid out at right angles, or else they make a village of their own, with every house in it exactly alike. The arid and empty plain of the Gohelle is full of life and industry now, and therefore not nearly so easy to fight in; modern armies find many obstructions, both offensive and defensive, due to the hand of man, where Condé had a clear field. Artillerymen use the pit-dumps as observation-posts or hide guns behind them; the infantry also finds them convenient for mitrailleuses.

Each mine, each village, each group of workmen's houses is made into a fortress; mitrailleuses peep from the air-holes of cellars; batteries lurk behind the shelter of walls. A long heroic and often handto-hand fight must be waged before any of these fortified centres can be taken; witness the assault of Vermelles by the French early in 1915, the storming of Loos by the English in September, 1915, and the fierce fighting which has been going on lately in the outskirts of Lens.

He set himself to outrival the Parisians who delight in airy wit and inconsequent paradox. In the forefront of Les Contemporains' he inscribed Sainte-Beuve's description of criticism as the flowing river that reflects the objects it passes, understands them, as it were, and exhibits to the curious traveller who floats on its bosom the changing spectacle along its course. He would reflect the literature of his own time. He would cast off the slough of professorship and pedantry, and be a modern of the moderns. Was it his fault, he asked, if everything in the literature of his day made him shiver with delight; if he loved it, mad, morose, restless, subtle as it was; loved it for its very affectations, absurdities, and exaggerations, the germ of which he felt within himself, and made his own by the study of it? After all, as he might also have asked, is one not a contemporary of one's contemporaries?

Accordingly, criticism should be an art of enjoying books, of enriching and refining one's own sensibility by means of them. And what about judgment? Ah, he would answer with smiling irony, he was so little of a critic; he did but note down his impressions. And these impressions, being individual, varied from month to month. Was not that natural? Nay, when M. Lemaître, his mental agility trained to its height, was occupied with his 'Impressions du Théâtre,' he could set contradictory impressions side by side, and tell you but to wait for the morrow and another change in his opinion.

If it was pointed out to him that he had preferences, which implied judgments, he retorted that M. Brunetière, delivering judgments with authority, had also his personal preferences, which he had but erected into a stately system.

If the dogmatic critic professes to judge against his own taste, he is himself content with tasting literature, and refraining from judgment. Or if―to continue speaking on behalf of M. Lemaître-it is easy to prove that he judges, and judges by æsthetical and moral standards, as we shall presently discover, he does not seek to impose his judgment, his personal opinion. He could not do so, convinced as he is that all things are relative, and that it is folly to require the agreement of any except the likeminded. That things are what they are, is apt to be the conclusion both of the philosopher who has accomplished the grand tour in the kingdom of ideas, and of the idler who shirks such toil.

But what of the dangers of such intellectual curiosity and unstable judgment? It would be as reasonable, perhaps, first to bear in mind its necessary limitations, or its disappearance with age and experience. M. Lemaître himself, receptive and suggestive to a brilliant and delightful degree, vivaciously exposes his own limitations, and his enjoyment of these limitations. It is M. Bourget, or an academic' critic like Montégut, who is capable of being cosmopolitan; it is M. Brunetière who can patiently make enquiry as to the theories of the 'Symbolists.' For his part, M. Lemaître will hear nothing of Scandinavians,

Russians, and the like; he is sure that one had the same thing done previously and better by George Sand and

Balzac, by Flaubert and Dumas fils. The dilettante must of course comprehend and reflect Shakespeare; but, after all, was Voltaire so very far wrong with his 'drunken barbarian'? As to the French writers who had the misfortune not to be modern, well-there was Racine, especially if you treat him as a contemporary. And as to these moderns themselves, M. Lemaître could not forget that he was a native of Touraine, shrewd, practical, sworn enemy of whatsoever was vague or exaggerated; and that he was a professor, a Frenchman, instinctively prompt to judge after the constant Latin-French tradition of classicism. Kindly of heart, he could not help presenting garlands of nettles to most of his contemporaries. If some of them seemed original, there was small wonder in that; they were so ignorant. A Don Juan of literature, as it were, admiring, professionally admiring, a thousand and three charmers, and all in all to each in turn, he reserves, in fact, his admiration for writers of well-considered thought or profound feeling. His theatrical criticism forcibly recalls him to decide upon moral questions; and for the solution of vexed problems he is not loth to offer his native practical wisdom, even that of the average householder, veiled in tender irony. His own dramas revealed him as fundamentally tender, not to say sentimental. In his 'Contes' he showed that he loved the simple and humble of heart and mind, who have the unspeakable merit of not being subtle and inconstant ; and that, a Latin as it were of the Fall, weary of philosophic systems, a neo-Latin of the neo-decadence, he harboured a 'piety without faith.'

After Alexander conducted expeditions into Judea and subsequently took many cities, he returned to Jerusalem. Following a three-year illness, Alexander died, and he left counsel for Alexandra.

When Alexander fled to the mountains, six thousand Jews gathered to meet him out of pity for his misfortune, prompted by Demetrius. This action alarmed Demetrius, who subsequently retreated from the region. Following this, the Jews engaged in battles against Alexander, but they were defeated and killed in large numbers during these conflicts. After capturing the most powerful of them in the city of Bethome, Alexander besieged them. Once the city was taken and the men were subdued, he brought them to Jerusalem. There, he committed an extremely brutal act: Howantiochus, known as Dionysius, ordered about eight hundred Jews to be crucified while he was feasting with his concubines, in view of the entire city. As an act of revenge for past injuries, he then ordered the throats of their children and wives to be cut before the victims' eyes.

Subsequently, Antiochus, who was called Thrace, though the narrator suggests he may have always been Dionysius and was Philip's brother, became greatly distressed by the dominion and the wars concerning it. He journeyed to Damascus because the power gained through these conflicts placed his reign in extreme jeopardy. As Antiochus waged war, his brother Philip heard of his predicament. Philip, initially content to fight against the threat, arrived in Damascus. At that time, Milesius, who had been left in charge of the citadel, had also come to Damascus with the same intention, and in fact, they had managed to reduce the Damascenes themselves to the point where they offered the city to Milesius. However, because Philip had become compelled to deliver the city back to the king of Arabia—a man to whom he was grateful for granting him the land of Moab and Gilead, which Philip had subdued—Milesius accepted the city. The Damascenes gave it up out of fear, rather than out of kindness or any other mitigating factor, and intended to reproach Milesius for not rewarding Philip.

Despite the belief that Antiochus should have committed this barbarity, it seemed to be done without necessity. Consequently, Antiochus was forced to leave Damascus again, taking the guise of a Thracian. Milesius then caught him marching toward the Jews. The soldiers who had been in the Hippodrome, numbering about eight thousand, rose up against him. They kept Damascus for Antiochus and, after Antiochus fled, the fugitives ran away that night. Eucerus, hearing of Philip's continued flight, returned from Arabia.

Social interactions at a gathering were complicated by social dynamics and individual emotional responses. Miss Canningham initiated the dancing, following Mrs. Harrington, which caused considerable surprise. This prompted Mr. Cunningham to advise Amy that since she was not in her own home, it was inappropriate for her to offer suggestions. Despite this, dancing began almost immediately. While others focused on the proceedings, Amy's internal state was preoccupied with the social slight. She felt neglected because she was not chosen to dance, even though she was present at a seemingly joyous occasion.

Amy observed that while many guests, such as Dora and Margaret, were the focus of attention, she was overlooked, deemed sufficiently at home to be left to herself and not important enough to be noticed. Despite the initial relief of not being forced to dance, the feeling of being ignored caused her significant distress. Her previous concerns had been overshadowed by recent varied and interesting activities, but now, while alone with Miss Morton, these old feelings resurfaced intensely.

She contrasted her own situation with that of Emily Morton. Amy felt a sense of isolation, intensified by the absence of her mother. She admired Emily Morton's quiet demeanor, noting that despite possessing beauty, elegance, and goodness, she was equally unnoticed. Emily possessed a disposition of quiet gratitude, viewing life's challenges as opportunities for self-improvement and blessing to others, a trait Amy deeply envied.

Amy attempted to emulate Emily's spirit, but the social pressure persisted. Even when Dora approached, and a few quadrilles were danced, Amy was still not asked to dance, leading to tears and a desire to leave. She was forced to remain quietly observing from the corner. Mr. Cunningham eventually approached her after the third quadrille, and his conversation provided a temporary relief from her loneliness, restoring a sense of pleasure. Amy perceived that his increased attentiveness towards her stemmed from overhearing what had occurred in the saloon, making her feel his kindness particularly after her disappointment. However, her ability to fully enjoy the evening remained diminished by the contrast between her high expectations and the actual experience.

The perception that the collapse of the Eastern question concerning Herzegovina is imminent is emerging, though the reasons for this—such as a reduction in news from insurgent sources—remain uncertain. This perceived development is being treated as a major morning sensation, and there is a desire for the associated headings, like "The Carlist War" and "The Insurrection in the Herzegovina," to cease appearing in daily journals.

This situation prompts a broader critique of the current state of journalism. The author argues that the inexactitude observed in reporting familiar foreign political subjects has led to a general distrust of these publications' views on more significant global issues. This pattern of inaccuracies is not isolated; from the Windsor conspiracy to the Porto Rico outrage, a series of errors has accumulated, strongly supporting arguments against the reliability of daily records. While acknowledging that mistakes are inevitable in the hurried, near-hourly editions of modern journalism, the author contrasts this with weekly journals, such as *The Athenaeum*, which traditionally maintained a high standard of factual accuracy, especially in literature. However, even *The Athenaeum*'s reliability has recently been questioned by its own inaccuracies, prompting contradictions and the publication of outdated, yet still imprecise, intelligence.

A specific instance of journalistic error is noted regarding the Prince's journey in India. *The Athenaeum* initially reported that Mr. Nassau Senior was going for the *Daily News*; this followed prior announcements that the chief of the "special" staff of the *Daily News* was too ill to travel and that Mr. Senior might be called upon. However, the person introduced was not the distinguished Mr. Nassau Senior, but a less notable staff member known for fishing sketches. Furthermore, even the fact of this Mr. Senior's journey has since been denied.

This general state of journalistic uncertainty is linked to international perceptions. If powerful nations like the Russian, Chinese, and Turkish emperors rely on English newspapers as translators for their own opinions, and if they only trust these papers when the views align with their interests—otherwise assuming the views reflect the government's—it is understandable that these foreign powers view England with suspicion, mirroring the distrust Englishmen feel toward other nations. This distrust directly impacts England's ability to maintain the highly valued peace, as reflected in the diverse editorial stances of major newspapers. The *Morning Post* exhibits Russophobia and worries about national apathy toward Russian actions near the Indian frontier. Concurrently, the philosophical *Spectator* expresses alarm over a potential rupture with China, advocating for a policy that might precipitate war, such as aligning with Japan or seizing Formosa. Even the *Examiner* has issued its own program, confidently predicting the downfall of the Turkish Empire, a scenario that most doubt can occur without European military involvement.

This constant stream of newspaper commentary—some fault-finding against foreign powers, others advising on necessary action—is creating a deeply uneasy atmosphere abroad. As this apprehension of danger grows domestically without a clear source or timeline, nations connected to Britain are likely to reflect this nervousness, preparing for potential conflict. Should war arrive, the time for regret will arrive, leading to pronouncements that mutual confidence, which many are now actively undermining, could have averted immense costs. Thus, the opportunity for peaceful counsel is now deemed critical, if it can be effectively urged.

Shifting focus to domestic culture, the author observes the recent exhibition of cartoons in the windows of low-class literature dealers, an event some deem treasonable, using the recent Solent disaster as a pretext. Despite this, the author believes the London populace, in general, is not prone to overly enthusiastic loyalty and is less likely than people in other regions to resent lampoons directed at prominent figures among them.

The narrative then shifts to a specific event involving the *Vanguard*, where Mr. E. J. Reed's analysis—drawing parallels to an essay on murder as an art—is mentioned. The author admires the "sally froid" of a Pembroke constituency member, who, after assessing the *Vanguard*'s unpreparedness against the *Iron Duke*'s swift, deadly attack, concedes that while the fight might have seemed evenly matched, the *Vanguard* failed to survive the blow. This writer concludes that while the wasteful and melancholic contest must continue, its origin lies in an essential beginning shared by man and Nature. The author suggests that while Reed's essay on evil may interest academics, English taxpayers prefer practical, cost-effective endeavors, implying that focus should shift from such abstract contests to domestic concerns.

Finally, in a diversionary anecdote, the author recounts a pleasant visit to Twickenham, where he spent time among anglers. While angling remains a major local pastime, the arrival of the Orleans family has altered the community's social fabric. Fishermen point to the three houses formerly owned by the Duc d'Aumale, the Count de Paris, and the Prince de Joinville, noting a local air of mourning for the departed Frenchmen, alongside some pride in their former status as hosts to royalty.

But not to their own band, chorus, and principals, should
the directors confine themselves, We see no reason why
they should not establish other amusements, hitherto
uncontemplated at the Crystal Palace-dancing, for instance.
What could be more appropriate than to have a ballet in
the very temple of statues and flowers? A good band, good
dancers, and a green curtain, is all that is wanted. The
Palace would supply its own scenery, and real flowers would
offer a pleasing variety. If we might be allowed to sug-
gest, we would recommend the ballet to take place in the
central transept during dinner-time, and a table might be
laid for five thousand people, all of whom, by a simple
arrangement, could witness the performance.
Above all, we would implore the directors not to take
Exeter Hall to Sydenham, nor make the special entertain-
ment provided in the Strand for subscribers to the
Sacred Harmonic Society a recreation for the multitude
in the Crystal Palace. None can accuse us of underrating
the importance attached to the performances of sacred ora-
torios, and the immense influence they exercise in the pro-
gress and appreciation of the best music. But everything
has its time and place. People go to Exeter Hall to hear
the Messiah, Elijah, the Requiem, or the Stabat Mater, and
for no other purpose. They are subject to no interruptions and
no distractions when the performance has commenced ; nor,
were they ever so inclined to be inattentive, is there any-
thing to interfere with their reverence and respect. Nay,
when the idle and the volatile-as will sometimes happen
from many causes-are induced unwittingly to step within
the precincts of the temple in the Strand, they are compelled,
by the absence of external attraction, to listen and affect
gravity ; or, better, they become insensibly interested, and
depart confirmed admirers of Handel. All this is very
different at the Crystal Palace. People go there to be
amused, to be recreated, to be refreshed, to experience as great
a number of sensations as possible in the shortest space of
time-to make a holiday, in short. To these the performance
of an oratorio would be no temptation, but the contrary. Of
course there should be attractions for all classes, Many, no
doubt, would be invited to Sydenham by the performance of
the Messiah, Elijah, or, The Creation, whom nothing else
would induce to pay a visit to the Crystal Palace. But the
great mass flock to Sydenham, leaving thought and occupa-
tion behind them, to enjoy the fresh air, see the beautiful
sights and hear the beautiful sounds-to walk among the
shrubberies, inhale the breath of flowers, and behold the
crystal fountains ; or, as Aretzus hath it :-
" Visere sepe amnes nitidos, peramenaque Tempe,
Et placidas summis sectari in montibus auras."
Except, indeed, on occasions of high festivals-anni-
versaries, and special commemorations, when the mind is
worked up to the proper tone of feeling-the proper attention
cannot be paid to large and serious works at Sydenham.
Everything around is antagonistic. The eye is bewildered
with enchantments; the odour of the flowers intoxicates
the sense of smell ; the mind insensibly wanders outside
to the grassy lawns and marble terraces, and wonders what
can possibly detain anyone within doors, when art and
nature are so prodigal of excitement without.

The author proposes a system for classifying the forms of flowers based on their relationship to the Sun. Flowers exhibiting a direct relationship to the Sun can be categorized into five primary patterns: reverberated, perpendicular, conic, spheric, elliptic, and plane or parabolic. Flowers with a negative relationship to the Sun correspond to five other patterns, which are presented in contrast to the first set. Despite the greater diversity in the forms of these negative flowers, all their variations can be traced back to the five positive forms.

The author suggests that if a set of specific accents were added to these five primordial flower forms to indicate modifications, a complete characterization of florification could be achieved, effectively creating an alphabet for a specific aspect of vegetation. Furthermore, this botanical alphabet could potentially be used to characterize different ecological regions on geographical maps. For instance, representing a reverberated perpendicular flower with an ear of corn or a prominent cone on a map could allow for the immediate identification of northern or high-altitude forests.

More specialized accents could distinguish between various types of trees, such as pine, epicea, laryx, and cedar, when applied to the general cone character. Rays issuing from these modified characters could then denote the geographic extent of those specific tree species. This system would allow maps to represent forests based on their composition, distinguishing them by species, while also indicating the latitude or soil elevation. The author argues this approach would eliminate the need for numerous political boundaries on botanical maps.

These maps would focus solely on natural domains, allowing viewers to instantly discern the natural produce of a soil, the variety of forests, and even the types of meadow vegetation. By incorporating characters representing the leaves and seeds of vegetables, the humidity or dryness of the territory could also be conveyed. Finally, ciphers, similar to those found on Turkish maps, could be added to cities and villages to denote population size. This integrated system would yield truly geographic charts that present, at a glance, an image of the territory's richness, climate, and population density. These ideas are presented as suggestions for further development and refinement.

Instances of intoxication demonstrate an individual's inability to manage or care for themselves. Public records have exposed the revolting language and disgusting behavior of certain aspiring statesmen. Measures have been implemented to prevent the recurrence of such disgraceful conduct, notably through the establishment of a temperance society in Washington, which includes members from both legislative houses. Although past experience has not fully confirmed the expected outcomes from pledges made by participants in such societies, they are viewed as valuable tools for helping those who might otherwise be lost and for alerting others to the severity of the problem and the dangers of its subtle influence.

During a recent Congressional Temperance Meeting in the Hall of Representatives, several Senators and House members strongly advocated for temperance. Among the speakers was ex-Governor Yates of Illinois, a Senator known for his eloquence but who was struggling with alcoholism. After declaring his commitment to sobriety, Yates shared a letter from his wife. In the letter, she expressed profound joy and felt a divine sense of relief upon learning of his resolution to abstain from intoxicating drinks. She described his self-conquest as the highest human achievement, affirming that those who loved him would support his pledge.

The powerful emotional impact of hearing such a description of the relief and joy felt by a devoted spouse witnessing a husband overcome addiction, thereby escaping the shame and wretchedness brought upon the family, was expected to be significant, hopefully motivating other struggling husbands. The text posits that human nature is inherently deceitful and desperately wicked, asserting that genuine and lasting personal reform is only achievable through Divine Grace, which addresses the source of evil and counters the tempter's deceptions. As individuals within a community experience this transformative power, immorality and folly should diminish within that community. Therefore, any human effort that encourages attention to and submission to this powerful regenerating force is deemed blessed. The author concludes that the only path to a radical and permanent cessation of intemperance is the widespread adoption of a practical belief in the religion of Christ.

The religious rites of Juggernaut were deliberately timed to coincide with festival seasons, seemingly to intensify misery. For instance, the abrupt shift from extreme June heat to heavy rains coincided with outbreaks of cholera among vulnerable crowds. Even amidst this suffering, the spectacle continued, featuring bands of music, dancers, and prostitutes of the lowest order, all contributing to the noisy, intemperate debauchery and profound pollutions found in the figures, exhibitions, and songs that constituted the worship.

Approaching the festival, the first sensations were those of horror and disgust, though these were intensified tenfold once the ceremonies commenced. The idol was displayed atop a towering car, which stood many feet high. This platform was adorned with massive, enduring sculptures depicting the most lascivious forms imaginable. Atop this structure sat the idol itself—a huge, misshapen block of wood, painted black with a bloody mouth, gold arms, and clad in rich, varied silk.

As the crowd surged forward, men, women, and children pressed to touch the ropes pulling the stupendous car. The priests and devotees bowed before the idol, employing indecent attitudes and gestures to seek its favor. The multitude erupted in loud shouts. Simultaneously, many pilgrims, worn out and travel-soiled, were crushed to death in the futile struggle, yet even in death, they seemed to greet their end with loud plaudits and a smile.

The idol finally began to move. The enormous wheels groaned under the immense pressure as the car rolled across the indented ground. After moving a short distance, it stopped, and the formal worship began. The chief priest then recited a long series of obscene and indecent verses, declaring that these were the songs that delighted the god, and only when pleased would the car move again. Following this pronouncement, the idol did move a few paces and then halted once more. Subsequently, a young man was brought forward to offer a propitiation that was even more lascivious than before, beginning to caper—a description too horrific to continue. In response to this display, a loud and renewed shout rose up from the multitude.

Attempts by Mr. Robinson's church to relocate to Holland involved several perilous undertakings. One attempt included hiring a ship in Boston to travel to Lincolnshire. After a significant wait and expense, the ship eventually arrived and took them aboard at night. However, the ship's master betrayed them, having previously coordinated with searchers and other officers. The group was seized, placed in open boats, searched thoroughly—even the women were searched beyond what was considered modest—and then brought back into town to be displayed to a large crowd. After being stripped of money, books, and other possessions, they were presented to the magistrates and committed to ward. Although the magistrates treated them courteously, they could not be released until the council issued an order. After a month in prison, most were dismissed and sent back to their origins, but seven key individuals remained incarcerated, bound over to the assizes.

A second attempt the following spring involved securing passage with a Dutchman in Hull who owned a ship belonging to Zealand. They hoped for greater trustworthiness in this Dutchman than in members of their own nation. The Dutchman agreed to transport them between Grimstone and Hull, near a large, remote common. They sent the women, children, and goods in a small hired bark, while the men were to meet them by land. However, they arrived a day before the ship, and due to rough seas and the women's sickness, the seamen brought them into a nearby creek where they were stranded on the ground at low tide.

The next morning, the ship was anchored but could not move until noon. The ship's master sent a boat to retrieve the men he saw walking on the shore. After the first group was aboard, the master noticed a large force of armed men, both mounted and on foot, preparing to take them. The Dutchman, upon seeing this, swore an oath of his country, weighed anchor, raised his sails, and departed while the wind was favorable. After enduring a severe storm at sea for fourteen days or more—during which they saw no sun, moon, or stars—they reached their intended haven near Norway. The people there gathered to celebrate their rescue from the harsh storm, which had caused significant damage. Some men who were in great danger managed to escape before the troop could find them, while the rest stayed to assist the women.

The plight of the women was severe, characterized by distress, weeping, and crying, some for husbands captured on the ship, and others fearful for themselves and their children. They were moved from place to place until authorities were unsure how to manage them. Imprisoning many women and their innocent children simply because they wished to remain with their husbands seemed unreasonable, yet sending them home was difficult because they claimed, truthfully, that they had no homes remaining, having sold or otherwise disposed of their previous residences.

In a separate matter concerning colonial governance, Edward Winslow petitioned the Lords Commissioners for the Plantations regarding encroachments by the French and Dutch. Winslow reported that the French had seized one of the colonists' houses and taken goods, while also killing two men and imprisoning the rest. Furthermore, the Dutch had established a fort on the Connecticut River within the boundaries of the colonists' letters patents, threatening to expel the English settlers from that river. Winslow requested that the Commissioners either secure peace with these foreign nations or issue a special warrant allowing the English colonies to defend themselves against foreign enemies. This petition gained considerable support. However, the plan faced opposition from Sir Ferdinando Gorges and Captain Mason, and the Archbishop of Canterbury. Gorges was intended to be sent as general governor, and the Archbishop sought to disrupt the religious proceedings of the colonists. Ultimately, the Archbishop halted the petition’s progress. Later, Winslow sought to have his suit granted, but the bishop, Gorges, and Mason managed to get Morton to file a complaint against Winslow. After Winslow defended himself satisfactorily to the board, they rebuked Morton and blamed Gorges and Mason for supporting the complaint. The bishop then questioned Winslow about his public teaching, which Morton alleged he engaged in. Winslow defended his actions as necessary to aid his brethren when a minister was absent. He also confessed to having married some of the women under his care, stating that marriage was a civil matter and not necessarily tied to a minister, noting that this was partly due to necessity, having lived together for a long time, and that he himself had been married in Holland by magistrates. Due to the bishop's strong insistence, the board eventually agreed to his commitment, leading to seventeen weeks of imprisonment in the Fleet before his release.
