Success depends upon a proper location, to avoid frost, quite as much as upon the nature of the soil. High rolling ground is preferred, since the colder air sinks by its greater specific gravity into the lowest place within reach, and the high points are not subject to the same degree of cold as the neighboring low places. Good apples are raised even on the "crawfish flats," especially on the highest points.

On the river bottoms, good fruit is sometimes produced (as in 1871,) when killed by frost on the adjoining hills. In this case it was probably protected by fog.

Black Locust grows quickly, and will produce a crop of good fence posts with some firewood every fifteen years.

Farmers object to its proneness to send up suckers on the adjoining ground; but they may be kept within bounds in groves on rough ground near the ravines, or on the steep hillsides that are worthless for other purposes. The trees should be four to six feet apart each way. If this course is followed, a fertile soil may accumulate on the barren slopes, when they are shaded by the trees and receive the addition of leaves each year. The cedar thrives on stony bluffs, and is recommended for such places; the larch has also been tried elsewhere if not in this district, and promises to be a profitable tree. Oak, Poplar and Walnut require at least a century to reach their full development, but future generations will require timber, and their needs should be regarded as well as our own.

The farmer's habits of observation enable him quickly to detect a field of natural fertility that has been worn out. By bad management it has been so changed that it will produce but one-half or one-third the crop that was raised on the virgin soil. The products are the criterion, rather than the appearance of the soil. By careful and judicious culture, on the other hand, the exhausted farm, or one not generally fertile, may be so improved as to yield double or quadruple crops. The changes, whether of deterioration or restoration, will depend upon the natural condition of the ground, the crops raised, and all those methods of treating the soil and crops that are embraced in the term, husbandry. I have sought to use every opportunity to converse with intelligent farmers and learn the methods they have used, the effects of such treatment and the systems which their experience enables them to recommend for this particular district. It is almost amusing to note difference of opinion on some of the simplest questions. One says that timothy improves the land; another, who is differently situated, that it deteriorates it, and that it was once as easy to raise two tons per acre as it now is to raise one ton on the same ground. One farmer recommends trench plowing, his crops having been improved by it; another tried it on the upland and years were necessary for the ground to recover its former productiveness.

The soil may lose its fertility, as we have seen, by taking the products off the farm each year, leaving less plant food in the ground for the next crop. This process has been carried on in a great part of this district. Some of the upland

has been exhausted by raising corn so that now it is difficult to get grass well set. The timothy crop has been impoverishing the soil more slowly, but not less certainly. It is estimated by chemical analyses that an average ton of timothy hay contains:

Although 142 pounds of mineral substance may seem a small matter to take from a half acre of ground, it must be remembered that some of these ingredients exist in very small proportions in the soil, and only a small part of these may be in a soluble condition ready to be taken up by the moisture and given to the plant. Is there any means to supply this deficiency? Some improvement is generally made where clover is sowed, especially if the green crop is plowed in. The vegetable matter, even of the roots, tends the loosen the soil, and admit the air and moisture to bring a new quantity of phosphates, etc., into a soluble condition.

Another plan, recommended for exhausted yellow soil of the upland, is to sow a crop of rye in the fall, clover in the spring, and turn in a drove of hogs in September for pasture. The rye will seed itself for the second year, when the hogs should be turned in again. Plowing in green manure and pasturing the ground are alike insufficient to add any mineral substance to the soil, and the most natural remedy is to use some fertilizer which will replace the elements removed. Stable manure is highly prized, and should be carefully husbanded; such a rotation is recommended that part of the farm be occupied by corn or wheat each year, and that these crops receive the manure. Rotten straw has been plowed under with satisfactory results. I am told that the improvement could be observed eight or ten years afterwards. Other fertilizers are needed to restore what is sold from the farm, and actual experiment alone will determine what is best adapted to the several conditions. A few experiments have been tried with lime, plaster of Paris, and other artificial fertilizers, but as a record has seldom been kept of the actual cost and of the probable improvement by increasing the crops, a great difference of opinion exists concerning the practical money result. A farmer's deliberate opinions deserves all due respect, but a strong prejudice seems to prevail among some who have never tried any fertilizer, that just as long as they can clear a margin beyond their expenses, the use of artificial manures is throwing money away.

Many farmers have told me that they see the increased growth of weeds or grass near a limekiln, or where a logheap was burnt. This observation is insufficient, however, to prove the value of lime, since the improvement may be due to the lime, or to the ashes which are rich in potash, and are known to be beneficial. A few farmers have applied lime to the soil, and generally have expressed themselves well pleased with the result; but an excess is injurious.

England alone has retained, until the last 35 years, the exclusive connection of centuries between education and the religious bodies; and (2) that England alone, in spite of all 19 the causes which, in our country as elsewhere during the last half century, have tended to increase crime, has seen its crime largely and steadily diminish. Individual figures here and there in statistics of crime may be shown to be affected by other and extraneous causes; but no ingenuity can evade the broad and striking fact that, while secular education, i.e. literary and scientific, has made equal progress and has been more perfected—as is generally asserted-in other countries than in our own, and all other causes, (drink, growth of . great cities, variations of employment, etc.) affect us equally, we English witnessed, till the end of the century, a steady and large decrease of crime, and all other nations have witnessed a steady and large increase.

I do not understand the mind of a man who, being confessedly unable to account for the fact otherwise, fails to put these two facts together, and to see in one the cause of the other. A statesmen would indeed hesitate to weaken the connection of education with religious bodies if he had this history and these facts present in his mind.

I should have expected a statesman also to have glanced at the criminal statistics for England and Wales for the latest year accessible, 1904, and to have noted the ominous words in the first page of the Introduction. "These figures are not all of equal value, as criteria of the state of crime, but they all indicate an increase of criminality in 1904.' "There has been a continuous growth of crime (indictable offences) since the year 1899." turn.

A statesman would reflect on the causes of crime, and consider whether, counteracting the influence of education, there has been in operation for a generation any cause which diminishes the influences which check crime at its origin, and is now revealing itself. The cause is not obscure.

Any superintendent of police would tell us that juvenile crime, and therefore in process of years adult crime, comes from what may be called "the residual areas"-the poor and neglected population that is not attached to any religious 20 body. We, churches and chapels, all of us, have our circles, some slightly overlapping of course; but mainly we all work at diminishing "the residual area."

The Roman Catholics, the Church of England, many of the Nonconformist bodies, the Salvation Army, have all been at this work, at " extension," and "forward movements"; and our work has told. We are not proselytising from one another; but trying to stop the ceaseless leakage into "the residual area." Now it is an undeniable fact, that voluntary schools and teachers in them have been among the means of stopping this leakage, and of attaching children to religious denominations; and, observe, not only to their own. I may say it has been the custom for us managers of the voluntary schools to see that all our children go to some Sunday School. I have never heard of an attempt—probably some have been made, though they are absolutely negligible to detach children from a Nonconformist Sunday School; but I do know that when such an inquiry revealed that in my late Day School at Rochdale some dozen or so of children were too ragged and irregular to be welcome even in our own poorer Sunday School (some dozen or so, that is to say, belonging to the "residual area, destined for crime), some members of my congregation promptly collected them for Sunday teaching. Now in great city Board Schools, it was shown at the time of the Jubilee in Salford that two children out of five are in no Sunday School. Such a result is inevitable.

It is nobody's business to look after them. The growth of schools not connected with any denomination means the growth of "the residual area," and means, therefore, the growth of crime.

## A Contemplation of Coniston: Where Nature Holds Her Own Domain

To travel amidst the celebrated Lake District is to partake in a pilgrimage to the very heart of England's sublime landscape. We have gazed upon the majesty of Windermere, whose sweeping vistas have long captivated the discerning eye, and witnessed the grand ascent of the fells surrounding Ambleside. Yet, as our journey proceeds, and the road begins its descent, a more intimate and singularly arresting scene unfolds before us—that of Coniston-Lake.

The spectacle begins with the gradual proliferation of the Coniston fells, which seem to multiply in number and stature, growing ever more striking with each mile traversed. Nearer to our vantage point, two low, rugged ridges, clad in the deep hues of purple heather and crowned with broken stone, march towards Ambleside, establishing curious precipices and chasms that speak of ages of geological labour.

Then, the road yields, and Coniston-Lake opens its bosom to the sightseer. Here, the dark, profound blues of the Furness fells rise from the northern margin, presenting themselves not with the precipitous drama found elsewhere, but in a bold, yet altogether more temperate manner. Our path guides us along the southern flank of this water, skirting its borders beneath a gentle, sloping ridge that mirrors, in a more unassuming fashion, the contours of the opposite shore.

This lake, stretching for six miles and possessing a breadth of three-quarters of a mile at its greatest extent, is a tapestry woven of indentation and repose. Its shores are gracefully scalloped, revealing succession upon succession of tranquil little bays. Interspersed along these banks are the humble dwellings of small farms, patches of venerable rocky common, and pockets of coppice-woods. Above this modest husbandry, the mountains ascend in sloping lines, draped in the verdure of summer, the rugged texture of heath, and the scatterings of stone.

Yet, it is in the character of this ascent that Coniston distinguishes itself. Here, the mountains do not present themselves with the tame, delicate screen-work one observes at the edges of Windermere, nor do they exhibit the grand, sublime, and awe-inspiring fronts that elevate their heads above the more commanding waters of Derwent or Ullswater. Instead, Coniston possesses a modesty of grandeur.

It is here, we perceive, that the pleasing hand of Nature seems to operate under a less stringent restraint. The wild strokes of her creation have not been so often marred by the intrusive touch of Art, nor have her simple, easy designs been so heavily embellished. Consequently, for those of us who seek the genuine article—the landscape untouched by excessive embellishment or the clamour of excessive visitation—Coniston-Lake offers a profound sanctuary. It is a place where one may pause, allowing the quiet dignity of the fells to settle upon the spirit, and find a more deeply personal communion with the eternal majesty of the hills.

An industry involving so large an output of produce, and in which there are so many problems demanding investigation, should certainly receive attention.

This is especially true of Illinois melons as found on the market. The quality of a melon is determined by various factors, but primarily by the condition of the vine at the time the fruit ripens. To produce melons of good quality, the vines must be properly nourished.

The best method of securing this end can be determined only by a series of carefully conducted tests in reference to kinds, amounts, and methods of application of fertilizer. It is important also that the effect of various methods of fertilizing, upon the earliness and yield of the crop be determined, since the profitableness of the crop to the growers is dependent largely upon secaring a large yield of early melons.

Tenth.-Even if a melon vine has been properly nourished by plant food, the quality of its product may be ruined by an attack of rust. This disease has done more to discourage growers and spoil the reputation of Illinois melons on the large city markets than any other single factor. In certain sections of the state (e. g.. in parts of Union and Marion counties) the melon crop has been one of the leading sources of income to the rural population. If melon growing is to continue in these sections, some practical means must be devised for controlling the rust. Otherwise, the industry is doomed.

ASTRINGENTS. The therapeutic application of this class of agents is confined principally to excessive morbid discharges, and relaxed conditions of particular parts. They are very frequently employed with great advantage in excessive mucous discharges, such as diarrhoea, dysentery, etc. In hemorrhage from the bowels following typhoid fever, astringents prove their medicinal properties. When applied locally with friction they prove successful in the treatment of many chronic diseases, such as tabes mesenterica, and dyspepsia when of an obstinate character.

If astringents are made use of for any length of time, either as internal or external agents, they tend to lessen the sensibilities of the parts with which they come in contact, and augment their density. This class of agents are contra-indicated when there is active inflammation with much febrile excitement.

BISMUTH.-Bismuth is not an agent of great power, yet when administered under proper conditions, the indications for its use being well marked, we find that it acts very kindly, and with great certainty. In irritation of the stomach, with determination of blood, marked by tendency to reject whatever is taken into the stomach, the tongue being red and pointed, with elevated papillæ, bismuth should be thought of as a remedy to allay the irritation, and place the stomach in proper condition for the reception and retention of other remedies. Uneasy sensations in the stomach, water-brash, and heart-burn, will usually yield to small doses of sub-nitrate of bismuth. In gastritis and ulceration of the stomach, it may be used with good effect to allay the irritation. In cancer of the stomach, combined with opium or morphine, it acts very kindly.

In the summer complaint of children it is a good remedy, controlling irritation and promoting digestion. In irritative diarrhoea the ammonia citrate (liquor bismuth) will frequently cure when agents of greater power have failed. In short, it is a remedy to be thought of in all irritable conditions of the digestive tract.

ACONITE. In the treatment of diseases of the digestive apparatus, aconite is an important remedy. In inflammation of the mucous membrane of the intestinal tract, by its sedative action and by its specific influence upon that coat, and its action upon the sympathetic nervous system, it gives relief by allaying the inflammatory conditions. It removes obstruction to the free circulation of blood, and favors secretion, thus preparing the parts for the kind action of other agents that may be required to entirely arrest the disease present. It should be given in small doses, and usually it is associated or alternated with ipecac. The indications for aconite are: The small, frequent pulse, or where there is evidence of enfeebled circulation of blood, increased temperature, nervous irritation, irritant diarrhoea and dysentery.

EUPHORBIA HYPERICIFOLIA has a specific curative influence on dis eased mucous membranes of the digestive organs: in diarrhoea, the discharges being greenish and irritating, with frequent desire to go to stool; irritation of stomach; dysentery, with evidence of irritation of mucous membranes; cholera infantum and sporadic dysentery, with greenish discharges, when inflammatory symptoms are previously removed. It acts as a tonic and mild astringent and very efficiently. R-Of the Tincture, gtt. x. to gtt. xxx. water 3iv., a teaspoonful every one or two hours.

THE CATHARTIC SALTS.-These act principally and specifically upon the intestinal canal. Having a greater specific gravity than the blood, they cause an endosmosis of the serum of the blood into the intestine, then, by distending the bowels and causing increased peristalsis. In their passage through the alimentary canal, a portion of the salt next the membrane becomes diluted and is absorbed.

Two conditions necessary to good digestion, and which the cathartic salts aid in bringing about, are, first, a healthy condition of the blood; and, second, a reciprocal action of the intestinal canal. During the progress of many diseases, and in torpidity of the bowels, the blood becomes loaded with impurities which prevent normal digestion.

These salts remove the disease-producing accumulations from the intestine, and, by exciting the intestinal exhalents, they act as depletives, not only freeing the blood of its detritus, but also increasing absorption and nutrition.

Derangements of the stomach from continuity of structure and sympathy, are overcome in this way. "All the salines rather depress the temperature," hence are not so dangerous in inflammatory states of the bowels.

As spring arrived, the natural world awakened. The sun rose earlier, the days grew longer, and the air warmed, bringing the sweet scents of budding earth and the sounds of forest life stirring from its winter slumber. Moose-birds sang their mating songs, jays and ravens preened in the sun, and the snowbirds gradually disappeared. Poplar buds swelled until they split, providing food for the partridges. Mother Bear emerged from her den with her young, teaching them to pull down saplings for the buds, while the moose descended from the high ridges, following the wolves that preyed upon the weak. Everywhere, torrents of melting snow rushed, ice cracked, and the earth and trees emitted dying frost-cries, while the Aurora Borealis crept closer to the Pole each night in fading glory.

At Wabinosh House, this spring brought particular joy, especially as Roderick Drew reunited with his mother. Before dwelling on the events of the preceding ten days—including the burgeoning love between Rod's mother and Minnetaki, the departure of soldiers after Rod's fight, or the gold hunters' preparations—the narrative focused on a specific evening in April. Wabi, Mukoki, and Rod assembled in Rod’s room, preparing for a long and thrilling journey into the far North the next morning. That final night, Rod slept little, overwhelmed by the fever of adventure. After the others left, he studied an old map until his eyes dimmed, his brain ceaselessly working in a half-slumber, showing him visions of a romantic cabin and a bag of gold nuggets.

Before the stars faded at dawn, the three men ate their last breakfast at the Post, a place that had housed families for two centuries. The factor maintained a cheerful mood, and even Minnetaki managed a smile despite her tears. After the meal, they went out into the cold morning air to the lake where their birchbark canoe awaited. Rod felt relief after bidding farewell to the two mothers, but Minnetaki joined them. When Wabi kissed her, she wept, and Rod held her hand, whispering a goodbye.

With a shout, Wabi shoved off, and the canoe sped into the gloom. Initially, the only sound was the rhythmic dip of the paddles. After a time, Minnetaki called out faintly, and they responded, but silence returned. Rod remarked that saying goodbye was the hardest part. Wabigoon replied that leaving Minnetaki was always hard, prompting Rod to excitedly suggest a future trip with her. Mukoki chuckled, praising her spirit. The young Indian then consulted his compass and suggested they cut straight across Lake Nipigon instead of following the shore.

Wabi, the old pathfinder, fell silent, causing Rod to ask if it was safe. Mukoki noted the south wind, which might strengthen, but Rod worried about the heavily laden canoe. Wabi urged them to risk the straight course, arguing that while following the shore would take half a day and half a night, crossing directly could reach the other side that same afternoon. Mukoki gave a reluctant assent, and Rod felt a strange sensation as the frail birch headed onto the vast lake. Their steady paddling carried them at four miles an hour, and by midday, the forest-clad shore of Wabinosh House was a hazy outline.

As the sun rose, its warmth and the sweet scents of the forests dispelled the chill, filling Rod with exhilaration. Wabi whistled and sang, Rod joined in with Yankee Doodle and The Star Spangled Banner, and even Mukoki expressed his happiness. All three men were united by a single thought: they were beginning the trail of gold, holding the secret of a great fortune, and their blood tingled with excitement at the prospect of discovery in the mysterious North.

The lake was populated with ducks, and the men shot several, until Wabi advised against wasting shells on them, reserving them for big game. After resting several times, they stopped paddling for over an hour at noon to eat lunch. The far side of the lake became visible, and as they resumed paddling, their attention turned to finding the mouth of the Ombabika, where their previous adventures had begun. Wabi pointed out a long, white rim along the shore, which he identified as swans. Mukoki, however, contradicted this, stating it was ice. This realization caused visible anxiety in both Wabi and Mukoki.

As the last days of March dawned, the countryside surrounding Rome was already vibrant, bearing the scent of June: the grass was tall in the Campagna, fruit-trees were in blossom, and roses and myrtles were in full bloom. Beginning an excursion from Rome, the travelers first journeyed to the "Fountain of Egeria," where they experienced a truly heavenly day. Their visit to the gigantic baths of Caracalla was brief; they paused for an hour in the shade of the arches, admiring the structures while simultaneously criticizing the character of their builder.

The journey then proceeded to the beginning of the ancient Appian Way. Shortly after, they reached the Tomb of the Scipios, situated on a hillside near the road. Upon arriving at the antique gate, marked by the inscription "Sepulchro degli Scipioni," the group found the structure more akin to a temple than a tomb. After observing the façade, they reflected upon the history of the Scipio family, realizing the significance of the place where the conqueror of Africa was brought from Rome.

Continuing along the Appian Way, the travelers drove toward the Catacombs. They entered the Church of San Sebastiano, which stood over the site where St. Sebastian was martyred. Inside, a handsome young Capuchin friar led them to the catacombs. After descending a long flight of stone steps into a low, damp passage, they encountered the tombs of the early Christian martyrs—nearly a hundred of them. This visit prompted a reflection on the humble dedication of Christ's followers compared to the grand works of the persecuting emperors. They then progressed to a small chamber, the site of forbidden Christian worship, where they observed an earthen altar and an antique marble cross, imagining the early believers praying there in secret.

Ascending back into the sunlight, the group moved on to the Tomb of Cecilia Metella. This structure, a stern round tower, was noted for its strength and its history of being converted into a fortress. From its lofty turrets, the travelers enjoyed a wide view of the Campagna, a vista considered by the author to be among the finest ever painted. Immediately below this tomb, in a flat valley, lay the ruins of what some call the "circus of Caracalla" and a small temple dedicated to Ridicule. Not far from these ruins flowed the Fountain of Egeria. The group descended into an antique chamber where the fountain emerged, its water crystal clear. The refreshing cool air, the growing flowers, and the vivid green of the surroundings made this spot an ideal place for contemplation, mirroring the inspiration felt by Childe Harold.

Finally, just above the fountain, on a hill crest, they found the thick grove believed to be the consecrated wood where Numa met the nymph. This secluded spot, surrounded by flowering fields, offered a perfect retreat for meditation. The excursion concluded as the travelers observed the general scene, noting that all the travelling world was now converging on Rome for the ceremonies of Holy Week, transforming the city into a busy, lively hub.

Katharine had been convinced of this for some weeks now, though Kenneth had said nothing. # The Shadow of Junius: A New Illumination in the Endless Pursuit of Truth

**By Our Literary Correspondent**

My dear readers, the annals of our literary history are often stained with the ink of mystery. Certain works, forged in the crucible of political fire, cast a shadow so profound that generations thereafter have laboured beneath it, forever seeking the true hand that guided the pen. The celebrated, and altogether enigmatic, Junius remains such a figure—a brilliant, venomous oracle whose pronouncements shaped the very temper of the age.

And now, once more, the relentless quest to pierce this veil of obscurity has advanced. Mr. Britton, in his latest voluminous endeavour, *Authorship of Junius elucidated*, has marshalled a prodigious effort to bring this long-dormant controversy into the sharp light of contemporary scrutiny. It is a monumental undertaking, one which demands not merely the diligent collation of facts, but the very alchemy of intellectual deduction.

The scope of this inquiry is nothing short of staggering. The author of this recent examination has ransacked the deepest recesses of personal anecdote and private history; minute details have been weighed against one another as if they were the weights of a celestial balance. Styles and language, those subtle signatures of the soul, have been subjected to the most rigorous anatomical dissection, even individual words brought into sharp contention.

Alas, the weight of this labour brings a profound, if familiar, melancholy. After this multiplicity of meticulous toil, the reader is left to wonder: how much ground has truly been gained? Even those scholars and political connoisseurs who possess access to the most guarded family annals and the secret repositories of political lore find themselves, ultimately, on equal footing with those who possess no peculiar advantage whatsoever. The central questions that vexed the learned minds of Junius’s day remain precisely the same; the catalogue of suspected names is refreshed, conjectures are hazarded only to be dismissed, and the same vague hope persists that some fortunate accident shall finally betray the identity concealed within the letters.

Among the names advanced through these meticulous researches, one figure appears with conspicuous vigour: Sir Philip Francis. It is curious, indeed, that this name seems to gain such prominence only in the later stages of this current investigation. For those who recall the initial, feverish hunts following the appearance of those elegant libels, Sir Philip Francis was absent from the pages of contention. We are informed that his name did not gain general traction until the publication of Mr. Taylor's work in 1816, a considerable span after the first suspicions took root.

Yet, it is not the newest candidate that demands our most considered attention. Long before the currents of modern speculation swelled, all eyes were fixed upon the esteemed Edmund Burke. Around him clung a conviction so tenacious that it resisted the might of the investigation. We are told that Doctor Markham, a man familiar with Burke’s earliest struggles—a man who watched with anxious hope his path toward honour—was resolved to secure an absolute denial from Burke, lest the stigma of Junius forever foreclose his advancement. We are invited to peruse a lengthy correspondence of Burke’s, a document said to illuminate the author’s own mind and the precarious state of his affairs at the time.

This brings us to a fascinating confluence of claims. Mr. Britton, in his systematic sweep, has not merely advanced new theories, but has revived the claims of a political figure of considerable eminence—a dedicated servant of the powerful Lord Shelburne. Though the chronicler admits he cannot declare himself entirely successful, he assures us that his arguments have been held in high esteem by able judges.

And what of Colonel Barré? His name stood prominently forward amongst the contenders, supported by the vigour of his talents, the ardour of his disposition, the character of his profession, and the web of alliances he maintained.

We must pause here, dear readers, to acknowledge the inherent frailty of such historical pursuits. When a subject is deliberately shrouded in such magnificent mystery, certain difficulties are inevitable. Circumstances will refuse to unite neatly; contradictions will demand reconciliation. For we are guided only by partial views, navigating a landscape where entire swathes of contemporary knowledge—the private whispers, the lost debates in the salons—have vanished into the ether.

Mr. Britton himself offers a sober caution, reminding us that time is a miser, secretly depositing its treasures upon neglected shores. Our materials are, by necessity, defective. Yet, even if Colonel Barré prove innocent, the work of Mr. Britton is not rendered vain. He has accomplished something no less significant: he has illuminated the terrain. He has furnished us with collateral information, removing obstacles from the path, making the subsequent traveller’s journey shorter and more lucid.

Indeed, Britton himself speaks of a trio of eminent politicians who shared the summers at Bowood—a place imbued with such political resonance. He has sought, through extensive reading and correspondence over the past twelve months, to acquire authentic evidence, accumulating materials that implicate not only the anonymous writer but also his intimate associates,

Political life experienced a period of Whig supremacy, during which the Tories, despite their strength in numbers and property, were marginalized, lacking prominent figures in business or debate, leading to a political atmosphere characterized by torpor. Administratively, two ministers brought distinction: Robert Walpole prioritized peace and prosperity, while William Pitt favored war and glory.

In society, the era presented a dichotomy: the age of princely patronage had ended, but the era of widespread intellectual intelligence had yet to arrive. Literary figures often faced destitution; for instance, a typical poet existed in squalid conditions, struggling financially, mirroring a fate that would have precluded earlier contemporaries from achieving comfort through writing, and that would deny contemporary writers commercial success. While a few authors, such as Pope (supported by legacy and initial patronage) and Thomson (who found subsistence through opposition ties), managed some stability, others like Richardson, Johnson, and Fielding, despite their talent, faced financial hardship. This shift in the writer's standing negatively impacted society, as government support tended to favor those engaging in low-level political libel, thus lending society a frivolous and material tone that persisted.

Morally, corruption remained prevalent, evident in both high and low places. In the House of Commons, members were notoriously susceptible to bribery, as exemplified by a minister successfully securing a vote through the promise of a large bribe, which the opposing member accepted based on prior favors. Private manners mirrored public failings, with "Money" being valued above honor and virtue. Although Richardson's novels began to refine societal tone, significant improvement in manners did not materialize until the reign of George III. Fashionable life remained coarse, evidenced by the social prominence of figures like dancing-masters and the grotesque entertainments of the time, which included elaborate, violent spectacles.

Public health and safety suffered gravely; gin consumption soared, reaching levels where it threatened the basic sustenance of the metropolis, a crisis the government temporarily failed to manage effectively. The general level of human decency remained low; executions were popular spectacles, with severe punishments administered frequently, sometimes publicly, and criminals often exhibited for profit. Furthermore, organized crime flourished, allowing thieves to multiply with operational structure, illustrating the unchecked impunity of the era.

Religiously, the educated classes increasingly imitated French elegance, leading to a decline in genuine piety. Butler observed that Christianity was being treated as a subject for ridicule rather than inquiry, and Warburton lamented that religion was losing its hold on the populace. The dominant religious discourse was cold and overly rational; preachers favored dry dissertations over heartfelt appeal, contrasting sharply with the enthusiastic, passionate sermons favored in France. Tillotson exemplified this dry style, presenting religious concepts as a logical proof structure. Consequently, while rational defenses of virtue existed, they failed to inspire true piety.

However, a genuine spiritual movement began to emerge beneath this superficial veneer. This revival started with a small group of Oxford students, led by John Wesley, who formed the Methodists. They deliberately moved away from abstract theology and polemics, focusing instead on direct, impassioned preaching about universal human suffering, eternal doom, justification by faith, and personal regeneration—tenets rarely heard from established Anglican pulpits. Their unstudied fervor contrasted sharply with the polished sermons of the time. Wesley’s reliance on divine guidance led to unconventional practices, such as reading the Bible randomly, reinforcing the idea that conviction, not mere intellectualism, constituted true faith. This spiritual awakening was paralleled by Whitefield’s itinerant preaching, whose passionate oratory moved enormous crowds. Whitefield actively sought out the marginalized, delivering the "bread of life" to vice-ridden populations, consciously reacting against the "colorless, marble polish of the age" by harnessing powerful human emotion for divine purpose.

Miss Dwyer, an Irish country girl whose dowry was traditionally meager, developed a profound interest in a grave, earnest child who posed singular, challenging questions. Miss Dwyer dedicated herself to developing her capabilities to meet this child's intellectual demands. The child, delighted to find an understanding confidante, began to share her hidden thoughts and feelings with Miss Dwyer. Under this lady's care, the child rapidly achieved a proficiency that astonished her instructress, demonstrating remarkable imaginative faculties even at a tender age; she would entertain her siblings with tales of her own creation, which soon delighted her parents as well. Her talent for improvisation soon made her a marvel in the neighborhood, transforming the once unnoticed child into an object of public interest.

Under the influence of Miss Dwyer's appreciative culture, the child's health improved, although her beauty remained undeveloped, and she was still known as the "plain child" of Mr. Power's family. Subsequently, circumstances necessitated the family's move to Clonmel, the county town of Tipperary. While the brothers and sisters anticipated this change with excitement, the child deeply deplored it, fearing the severance from her cherished childhood scenes. On the morning of the departure from Knockbrit, she went to her favorite garden and gathered a large bunch of flowers to keep as mementos of the place. Fearing mockery from her unsentimental siblings, she hid these treasures carefully in her pocket. Upon arriving in Clonmel, the other children drew admiration with their appearance, but the timid Marguerite was overlooked until the lady of the house noticed an unusual projection in her pocket. When questioned, the silent child was led to show the withered flowers. Amidst the assembled laughter, these flowers were tossed contemptuously out the window. The poor girl reacted with sorrow, and her grief was compounded by reproof for weeping over the destruction of her treasured items, illustrating how poorly her keen sensitivities were understood by her relatives.

The move to Clonmel initiated a string of misfortunes for the family. Mr. Power began speculations that proved ruinous. Two of the children died shortly after each other, and generally, "everything went wrong." Despite this, Marguerite and her sister, Ellen, whose beauty had now reached parity, began engaging in society at Clonmel, drawing attention. While the 47th Regiment was stationed there, two officers, Captain Murray and Captain Farmer, both declared admiration for Marguerite. Marguerite developed an intense aversion to Captain Farmer, sensing an evil influence. Captain Murray proposed to her, warning that Captain Farmer also intended to propose. Marguerite's dismay intensified when Murray revealed his rival suffered from hereditary insanity. To her horror, she soon learned that Captain Farmer had proposed to her parents, who had agreed because the proposal included significant settlements, a tempting prospect given Mr. Power's financial struggles. Thus, at the age of fourteen and a half, the girl was forced into this unwanted marriage. Captain Farmer soon discovered her aversion and subjected her to brutal persecutions based on unfounded jealousy. Eventually, terrified by his increasing fury, she fled his home forever. Her parents, showing little natural feeling, refused to shelter her at that painful time.

Fortunately for Lady Blessington, Captain Farmer’s life was brief. In 1817, during dinner, he was seized by one of his insane fits. Unable to force open the locked door, he rushed to the open window and threw himself out, dying instantly.

Lady Blessington’s beauty, now in full bloom, attracted many suitors. She eventually chose the Earl of Blessington, marrying him in London in March 1818. This change in fortune allowed her lavish nature to flourish. She repaid her parents, who had coerced her into the miserable marriage, with a generous allowance that continued until their deaths. She became a prominent figure in society, hosting gatherings in the salons of the Countess of Blessington, where distinguished men of the day were encountered. Her refined taste in dress was matched by the resources of wealth that allowed for costly extravagance. Shortly after their marriage, she toured Italy with Lord Blessington, during which time she befriended Lord Byron. Her travel impressions formed the basis of her best published work, "The Idler in Italy."

In 1825, Lord Blessington died in Paris from apoplexy. Lady Blessington remained in Paris until after the Revolution of 1830, after which she returned to England, ultimately settling at Gore House in Kensington. When circumstances later forced her to relinquish this residence, a sale was held, drawing crowds of the curious. After dissolving her establishment there, she traveled to Paris again, taking possession of a beautiful apartment on the Champs Elysées in April 1849. Whether due to the change in location or overexertion in managing her new home, the result was sudden and melancholy. On June 2nd, she entered her new abode; the next day, she suffered from difficulty breathing. Despite all medical intervention, she gradually deteriorated and died the following day, June 4th

At Sens also there was an exhibition of atrocious fanaticism: during three successive days the bell of the cathedral invited the citizens to murder.

Will you kindly correct a slight mis-statement in your reviewer's notice of Uncle Tom's Tenement'? It is said, 'some satire is directed against the "fashionable philanthropy" which collects its rents from tenement-houses until it pays to turn its capital into something else.' No such case ever came under my observation, and there was nothing anywhere in the book intended to give that impression or suggest that idea. So far as any such connection was attempted, the effort was to show precisely the reverse: that capitalists leave other investments for those in tenement-houses which pay better than almost anything else, and then in the charm of lucrative investment forget to consider the rights of their tenants.

The matter is of but slight importance, perhaps, but as that is the only statement your reviewer makes as to the contents of the book, I should like to have it correct. Current Criticism A FASCINATING CHARACTER.-Mr. Cabot's biography of Em erson gives a fascinating picture of a fascinating character. Apart from individual facts and utterances, it contains little that is new.

It supplements rather than essentially modifies the conception of Emerson based upon his writings and upon previous records.

There was no secret to tell, no mystery to solve. Mr. Cabot tells the story of a limpid life, without rapids, without eddies, without turbulence of any kind. The only secret about Emerson is one that never can be revealed-the secret of his ineffable opticism, his power of living upon phrases. This is an ultimate fact of character, defying analysis; and it constitutes at once the greatest charm and the greatest limitation of his genius. The unruffled azure of Emerson's mind suggests the Blue Grotto at Capri or some such freak of nature rather than an open-air stream flowing freely along and mirroring the storm cloud as well as the empyrean, the baleful meteor no less than the steadfast stars. Mr. Cabot's memoir merely proves what needed no proof, that this peculiar habit of mind was neither assumed nor acquired, but inate and ineradicable.

A great uproar also prevailed, and the mob evinced the strongest intentions of preventing, by force, if necessary, the mutilation of the towers of their beloved Minster. The authorities, however, had been forewarned of their approach, and as forewarned is proverbially forearmed, set out in defence of the Close and the Minster. The gates were hurriedly closed and secured, and men placed at each to guard them against the expected attack.

Strangely enough, the little postern gate at the head of the stairs was left unguarded, either because it was overlooked in the haste of the defensive preparations, or because it was expected that this would be the least likely to be the scene of assault, and the none too large body of defenders congregated elsewhere. With comparative ease, therefore, the assailants battered down the gate, and surged through into the Close, creating a deafening din, which re-echoed strangely from the walls of the Minster, looming vast and high above them in the half-darkness. Some of the mob rushed into

Vicar's-court, where they attacked the house of one of the "Old Vicars," Mr. Cunnington, who was Receiver-General of the Chapter, and acted as a kind of secretary, treasurer, etc., all rolled into one.

Mr. Cunnington was at home, and the mob entered his house, and seized him, dragging him thence to the Minster Green, where they are stated to have formed a ring round him, and goaded him into dancing for their diversion. The Minster Green, it is affirmed, rang with their cry: "High Church, Low Church, Jump again, Cunnington !"

At any rate this demonstration had the desired effect, for an assurance was given, and published abroad by the Town Crier the next day, to the effect that the Dean and Chapter would respect the wishes of the citizens, and that the spires should remain unmolested.

The Chancellor, who probably knew the class of people forming the mob very well, opened his beer cellars, and the rioters refreshed themselves after their exertions. The gates were then thrown open, and the mob dispersed with more or less quietness. Whether any recompense was accorded the unfortunate Receiver-General is not stated, but he certainly deserved considerable compensation. both for the injuries bestowed on him and for the loss of dignity in the disgraceful scene on the Minster Green.

It is curious to note the difference between the conduct of the townspeople on this occasion and less than a century later (in 1807), when the Dean and Chapter decided upon the same act of vandalism as their predecessors, and, what is more, carried it out, to the great regret of many who admired the lofty, graceful spires. ## A Landscape of Contrasts: Monaghan and the Unfurling Thread of the North

One travels through this rugged quadrant of the island with a spirit perpetually in motion, seeking the subtle delineations that separate one character from the next. Yet, it is in a modest settlement such as Monaghan that the traveller is struck not merely by geography, but by a profound and arresting collision of temper and custom.

This town, possessing a certain quiet dignity, anchors itself firmly within the industrious spirit of linen and sundry mercantile pursuits. The populace, predominantly of the Presbyterian faith, gather in a place of worship—a structure of pleasing sobriety, eschewing the gilded excess favoured elsewhere. But to step from the familiarity of one neighbouring burgh into Monaghan is to endure a sudden, startling disquiet. Indeed, the transition is akin to waking suddenly from a dream of London’s clamour only to find oneself deposited abruptly within the air of Edinburgh. The very cadence of speech, the set of the gaze, the ingrained habits of the citizenry—all seem to articulate a distinct and compelling difference.

Monaghan, it seems, occupies a curious threshold; a frontier where the peculiarities of the North begin to manifest with a resolute vigour. For the ear accustomed to the dialects of the Irish heartland, the local tongue presents an immediate, discernible signature. An Englishman, perhaps, might hastily affix the label of mere Scotch, yet such a judgment is fatally incomplete. This accent, like the very temperament of its people, is not wholly of one parentage, nor entirely of the other, but a rich and complex admixture of both.

Indeed, the history of this portion of the kingdom whispers tales of great migrations. A significant portion of the inhabitants owe their lineage to those Scots who found their way hither following the ascendancy of James the First upon the English throne. And what a tenacity they possess! It is almost difficult to conceive how so pertinaciously they retain the customs and usages of their forebears, were it not for the peculiar circumstances of their settlement. They were established amongst a native population whom they held in disdain, whose natural talents they seemed to dismiss, and whose religious convictions they scorned.

In other maritime counties lying opposite the shores of Scotland, the tide of displacement was tragically absolute; the native population was nearly swept away. There, the Scotch mannerisms endured with a startling, almost primitive freshness. Monaghan, however, presents a more nuanced tableau. The subjugation of the native element was complete in its finality, yet the process of expulsion was by no means so sweeping as in those coastal towns. The new arrivals claimed the most fertile valleys and the most accessible stretches of land, yet they showed a certain measured courtesy in leaving the native population to the rugged contours of the bogs and the higher mountains.

As the initial rigours of their dominance waned, and as the fear that once animated their posture began, by degrees, to subside, the complex tapestry of Monaghan—of its mingled tongue, its blended character, and its settled landscape—remains a profound study in the tenacious ways that human spirit adapts, endures, and weaves itself anew upon the soil.

Petrarch is a figure of enduring significance, constantly being celebrated and analyzed, much like Shakespeare. His contribution to the advancement of erudition and ancient literature, along with the cultivation of taste and genius, is considerable, even when compared to his predecessors and successors such as Dante and Boccaccio. Early accounts of Petrarch's life, particularly those published in French and translated, offer some intriguing details, though these are often presented without clear order and mixed with speculative claims. Historical records from the 14th, 15th, and 16th centuries, including those by Alexander Vetutello, provide limited reliable information because fable is frequently interwoven with truth in these accounts. Other Italian and foreign writers who have documented Petrarch's life, with varying degrees of success, include Gesnaldo, Tomasini, Schoderen, Philippe van Maldeghen, Catanusi, Beccadelli, Muratori, the abbe de la Bastia, and others. Furthermore, a manuscript life of Petrarch, written by Lelio di Leli, a descendant of a friend of Petrarch, is believed to exist in the Ambrosian and Ricardinian Libraries, but it has never been published or consulted by biographers.

The current work, authored by Giovanni Baptista Baldelli, aims to present a comprehensive biography of Petrarch by gathering authentic facts about him, while also offering observations on the state of literature during his time. The introduction details the literary portrait of Italy, which is subsequently elaborated upon with an examination of the political situation and the civil wars in that part of Europe. The first two books of Baldelli's work are dedicated entirely to the early years of Petrarch, focusing specifically on his love for Laura, a theme that has secured his lasting fame through the admiration inspired by his writings centuries later. The third book discusses Petrarch's influence on the political affairs of Italy, while the fourth examines his contribution to scientific progress, his profound impact on the nation's taste, and his literary network of friends and protectors. An appendix titled "Illustrations" contains detailed chronological accounts pertaining to the poet's life and the eminent figures connected to him. Baldelli bases his remarks and notes on these points on both ancient and modern authors, resulting in a biography that is claimed to be the most complete, authentic, and thorough of its kind up to that point.

## A Nocturne in the Alps: Reflections Upon an Evening in Evolena

The journey through the alpine passes, that grand pilgrimage of the intrepid traveller, often presents trials more taxing than the ascent itself. One anticipates the rugged majesty of the peaks, the crystalline purity of the streams, yet seldom does one prepare for the domestic adversities—the chill of a refusal, the discomfort of an unexpected lodging. It was such an encounter in the little town of Evolena that cast a somber, yet richly human, shadow upon our passage.

We found ourselves, quite unexpectedly, denied the solace of a bed. The pronouncements were swift: lodging was impossible in the Cure. A vexation, indeed! In the course of that evening, our thoughts drifted, with a sweet, melancholic longing, toward the deserted chalets of Prarayon, those silent dwellings from which we had drawn our temporary respite the preceding night. How vividly, one might say, we envied their solitary grandeur, for the amiable household of Monsieur A at Val Pelline seemed, by contrast, to belong to some other, perhaps more graceful, order of existence.

The day had been marked by a subtle ill-fortune; our faithful companion, Klaus, succumbed to a malaise during the latter hours. Yet, necessity, as ever, dictates our immediate conduct. We were thus confined to a humble table, dressed as we were, enduring two hours before a simple soup, prepared with our own stores of rice, was finally served.

As the gloaming deepened, a flicker of hope appeared. Word reached us that a single bed might be secured within the village. We abandoned the Pfarrhaus with a grateful haste, shaking the dust of the road from our boots, and proceeded to the designated lodging. The inhabitants proved civil, and possessed a tolerable degree of cleanliness, though their local idiom presented an impenetrable barrier to our understanding. It was revealed, with a degree of local severity, that but one spare cot existed in the entire village. By the lot—that most ancient arbiter of fate—the prize fell to me. The bed itself was Spartan, lacking both softness and perfect levelness, yet between the relentless demands of such protracted travel, even the simple act of undressing ranks among the most profound luxuries. I slept soundly into the following morn.

It was M. Studer, upon entering my chamber, who broke the quietude. He confessed a night of profound misery, and consequently declared his immediate intent to depart for the Val d'Anniviers, foregoing the leisurely contemplation of the Evolena region. While a pang of regret stirred at his departure, one could not gainsay the propriety of his resolution. He left shortly thereafter, and we settled upon the agreeable arrangement of meeting at Zermatt—him proceeding via Visp, and myself by Ferpecle.

Before the final act of dressing could be accomplished, our worthy guide from Val Pelline presented himself to bid us farewell. During the previous day’s ramble, a quiet understanding had been forged between us; his inherent simplicity of character touched us both deeply. He had expressed on several occasions a desire to accompany us further afield, perhaps even to avoid the circuitous route of his own homeland. Though now he spoke no such petition, he bid a quiet adieu and took the road toward Hauderes.

Watching his figure recede into the distance, a distinct sense of regret overtook me. One could not help but muse upon the utility of such a companion on the more arduous stretch of our journey ahead. My own servant, though diligent, possessed insufficient experience for the terrain; and the guide of Arolla, though promising in his assurances, remained a complete unknown to my acquaintance. Thus, the amiable departure of a known, gentle soul added another layer of melancholy to the tapestry of our alpine sojourn.

## The Honourable Conduct of the Reay Fencibles: A Study in Military Virtue

**A Chronicle of Discipline and Distinction amongst a Regiment of Gentlemen**

In an age where the rigid confines of military service are often perceived as breeding ground for vice and dissipation, it is a curious and most pleasing subject to examine those regiments whose very existence seemed to uphold the highest ideals of gentlemanly conduct. Such is the case with the Reay Fencibles, whose brief tenure amongst the Irish populace offers a most admirable portrait of soldiery elevated by inherent honour.

It is often remarked that the soldiery, by its very nature, risks straying from the paths of elevated society. Yet, the discipline and character of these particular officers and their men presented a pleasing counter-argument. Possessing sufficient means, it is noted that they employed their liberality not in wanton excess, but in the manner befitting men of good standing. Indeed, they maintained the necessary funds to pursue their social amusements with a decorum that would spare the judgment of the most fastidious society.

A frequent and commendable practice amongst them was the subscription to entertain their acquaintances. These soirées were not confined to the austere confines of the barracks, but were frequently given in public rooms—venues they possessed the good sense to hire. To these gatherings, it must be noted, attended not only the officers of the corps but also many respectable inhabitants of the towns where the regiment was quartered. These civilians, drawn by curiosity, were equally moved by a profound satisfaction at witnessing men conduct themselves in a manner that lent true credit to the noble profession to which these soldiers belonged.

The standard of rectitude among the core of this regiment was, in truth, exemplary. Amongst these men, those crimes which necessitate the severest of punishments were, by all accounts, unknown. Indeed, the gentlemen would have regarded any punitive degradation—such as a banishment from their native country where they might not dare appear in the daylight—as a fate most intolerable. This internal commitment to honour speaks volumes of their breeding and their moral fibre.

Now, the annals of any military posting are rarely without their blemishes. During the seven years the regiment was stationed in Ireland, there were instances of desertion and corporal chastisement. Yet, a careful reading of the record reveals a crucial distinction. These transgressions were committed by men who were not originally enlisted in the corps; they formed a separate, discordant party, one with whom the "standard and original men of the regiment would not associate."

Had it not been for the presence of these few discordant elements, the entire corps would have enjoyed the satisfaction of returning to their native glens without a single man having suffered disgrace. But the commendable spirit of the regiment remained untarnished by the failings of others, for those degraded men were not of their own country or kindred.

Thus, the tale of the Reay Fencibles serves as a gentle reminder to the discerning reader: that even within the disciplined ranks of the armed forces, the virtues of honour, sobriety, and gentlemanly society may flourish, offering a model of conduct worthy of our highest approbation. They were eventually removed to Scotland, and the regiment was reduced in the year 1802, yet the memory of their honourable bearing shall long endure.

Modern culture owes very much, again, to these Cambridge scholars who trained the Elizabethans and others. The new

England which Wyclif, Chaucer, Bacon, Shakespeare created has always recognised its debt. It does not forget; or perhaps we can hardly say that, even so soon as two centuries ago, it set itself seriously to measure itself and its own intellectual achievements. This measured measurement is especially true of one great point which should distinguish our modern England from the England of Elizabeth-a point of fundamental import, that may appear sufficiently obvious. A distinction has always been maintained, of course, between the learning of the day and the literature of it: I need only instance the case of Shakespeare. One may venture to think it a somewhat artificial, nay, a rather artificial and fanciful distinction; and it will hardly stand minute examination. But let it stand! The language and the thoughts of Shakespeare, so the critics say, so the lovers of literature tell us, differ vastly from the language and thoughts of the most conspicuous poet of his time and generation: we may almost say that Shakespeare could not write. Even such a critic as Tennyson is found once to hint that Shakespeare's power of expressing himself in English was an accident. However it came about, and however, if so one must say, it has been explained, Shakespeare himself must not only have written better plays, but he has, for generations since, been the favourite writer with every stage-going child. It matters not if a great deal of what Shakespeare wrote was really so thoroughly unintelligible, in one sense, at least, to himself, that it could have been read as readily by a dictionary as by his poems themselves; we see for ourselves how he understood his audience, and the audience, being right-hearted and well-read as they were, has become, we may fairly hope, the best interpreter possible of Shakespeare's meaning in his day and of the best ideas of the people, at least, in our day. So we find ourselves wondering what his idea was, and, as he himself saw far beyond this period of England and this age, we have no doubt he would have explained to us as to ourselves what the language of his time might mean and what it meant to him: only his great contemporary, Bacon's, English would not convey his idea, though his method of putting it and expressing it would have been quite plain enough for his own age, which was an age of such high intelligence, with all men's minds quickened and cultivated.

In a similar way, we may see, our own contemporary literature does not greatly help us to apprehend the mind of to-day: however fine, subtle, subtlety and insight, may be our minds, there is always something lacking in our notions of thought and life; though there may be much to be taught us, even this kind of thing, the art of thinking, is still a thing too unfamiliar and new for our minds; we can learn far more about it in our own century than in many hundred years before. To feel it for oneself is easy. But let him try to understand literature who finds so far that its language does not go in tune with the language of to-day. It is, then, in the spirit of all this that modern English scholarship regards and seeks to make manifest these two facts, the need of teaching and the necessity for studying literature and life to bring out its best influence. To these objects scholarships and examinations aim. We are only here to indicate it briefly and to point a little in the same direction.

Caroline crossed the threshold, and his harried expression relaxed to one of interested recognition. Here was the young lady who had always put him in mind of Miss Dawson-he had heard she was back from foreign parts and married; but she wasn't a patch on

Miss Dawson now-no color in her cheeks and not 'alf enough flesh on her bones. "The boy was just going round with the order, miss," he hastened to explain, assuming she had come in irate pursuit of the holly and the oranges that had been promised for not later than four o'clock, and were still reposing in a basket by the desk.

Caroline reassured him rather diffidently. Sojourn in India, where white people of a different class are seldom encountered, sometimes creates a slight feeling of awkwardness in those who have lately left the country towards such people, just because they are English. Caroline was now vaguely conscious of the sensation, and she remembered a laughing admission of her grandfather's - that he had never known how to address the maidservants when he first arrived home! "How is Mrs. Blake?" she inquired. "Lady Wendover has sent her something for her cough," and she tendered the little parcel.

Poor Sam Blake looked troubled and apprehensive. The errand - boy stopped working and stared with round eyes, his cheeks inflated, the picture of stupidity. "She's very bad, miss, I'm afraid, and she won't let me send for the doctor. She went upstairs after dinner, and there's been no time to see to her since." He hesitated helplessly, and Caroline divined the relief it would be to the young man were she to offer to go up and reason with his mother.

It crossed her mind that Mrs. Blake was apparently as difficult and irrational in sickness as was her own grandmother. "Would you like me to take the medicine up to her and see what I can do?" she suggested, on an impulse of sympathy.

Sam snatched at the proposal; his mother might listen to "class," though she refused to "mind" anything he could say. He hastily opened a door at the back of the shop and invited her to climb a steep wooden staircase covered with cracked linoleum. "The door on the first landing, miss, and mind the steps," he said gratefully.

Above the mantelpiece was a stuffed pheasant in a glass case. Everything was clean and tidy and in order, but so depressingly unattractive-like superior "apartments." From the inner room came the sound of someone speaking loud and fast.

Caroline peered between the curtains into a room of much the same description, only that it was more elaborately furnished with basket chairs and whatnots, and bamboo tables, and a multitude of little ornaments. Mrs. Blake, a knitted shawl over her shoulders, was seated by a fire that burned badly in a high, old-fashioned grate. All her spruceness was gone, her still luxuriant hair looked dull, and hung in wisps about her face; there was something flaccid in her attitude and appearance, as though the motive-power of sense In and energy had been withdrawn. her shaking hands she held a photograph and she was talking to it unnaturally. In the eight years since the first edition of this book appeared, it has established itself as one of the standard text-books on the subject. We may mention a few criticisms which occur to one in reading the volume.

The specific microbic origin of chancroid is regarded as still unproved, Ducrey's bacillus not being accepted by the authors as such. Cock's operation for retention of urine from stricture is mentioned but not described, and the same applies to Peters's method of transplanting the ureters into the rectum in exstrophy of the bladder; both are worthy of being given in more detail. In enlargement of the prostate the use of the various intra-urethral instruments for diagnostic purposes seems to be rather lightly undertaken, in view of the risk of introducing infection.

Removal per urethram of pedunculated vesical tumours can be more accurately accomplished by means of the combined cystoscope and écraseur than by a lithotrite. The description of nephrectomy is confused, and there is an error in connection with the freezing-point of urine. These, however, are small points taken at random, for the book is written carefully and with full attention to detail. The descriptions of the anatomy and physiology of the various parts of the genito-urinary apparatus are useful without being too long. The diagrams and photographs are good, but the coloured illustrations of syphilitic eruptions and cystoscopic fields in the bladder serve, by comparison with the uncoloured, to show how difficult it is to convey a proper idea of such things by uncoloured drawings; the plate of urinary calculi, however, has rather too many rainbow colours. This is one of the few books published outside Scotland which recommend the Sprengel pump principle for bladder drainage; it is described here as Dawbarn's method, though Cathcart's name is mentioned. There is a long chapter on

urinary symptomatology, and a full description of the examination of the urine, and of other methods of urinary diagnosis, such as cystoscopy, segregation of the urine, catheterisation of the ureters, and the various other means of testing renal capability. As regards prostatectomy for enlarged prostrate, the balance is held evenly between the perineal and suprapubic routes, some cases being suitable for each method.

A large amount of space is naturally devoted to venereal diseases, syphilis claiming more than one-fifth of the whole volume. In the preface the authors state that symptomatology, diagnosis, and treatment are the primary objects of the book, not pathological questions, especially where not definitely settled. This has excluded any discussion regarding the cause of syphilis, and the Spirocheta pallida, though depicted in a coloured frontispiece, is not mentioned in the text. Syphilitic skin. eruptions are very fully described and illustrated. Constitutional treatment of the disease in a typical case may be summarised as follows:-No mercury till the diagnosis is established; then mercury continuously for two years, six weeks of mouth administration alternating with a fortnight of inunction; then mercury and iodides for the next six months, and iodides alone for any tertiary manifestations. Excision or cauterisation of the primary lesion, if seen before lymphatic involvement, is regarded as a justifiable and in a number of cases a successful abortive measure.

The book can be thoroughly recommended, but reference would be simplified if more separate headings were included in the index.

SIM WALLACE has constituted himself the champion of the hypothesis that dental caries is caused by the consumption of "pappy food, and may be prevented by the substitution in childhood of articles of a "fibrous" consistency. The hypothesis is based on large assumptions, and a liberal amount of circular argument has been expended in its support. By like assumptions and arguments the cause of dental caries may as convincingly be found in Vaccination, Compulsory Education, or Free Trade. It appears there are still, strange to say, some doctors and dentists unconverted to the author's views. He therefore returns to the charge with these supplementary essays on the cause and prevention of dental caries. Dr. Wallace's mental attitude to what he calls pap food is only comparable to that of the schoolboy who wrote in his "Essay on Pins": "Pins has saved many lives by people not swallowing them." He does not strengthen his case by constant reiteration of his argument or by the tone he adopts to other authorities, to whom he is unjustifiably patronising or contemptuous.

His little book requires revision. Corpus Ville (p. 2) is not Latin ; neither is it a printer's error, for it occurs again on p. 79. "Over six years have elapsed since my investigations. was published," is not a grammatical sentence. The following paragraph, with its conditional invocation of Divine aid, is quite superfluously vulgar:-"So again I must regretfully admit that in America the great dictum that the

'toothbrush is mightier than the dentist' still reigns supreme. If the dictum be correct, God help the dentist!"

Perhaps the ignis fatuus is meant. The author says (p. 78): "If in recent years medical men have been able to inflict a restricted, soft, alkaline, insipid, unphysiological, and even repulsive diet on the vast majority of children, is it not possible that they will in the future be able (with the aid and advice of the dentist) to impose a less restricted, less pappy, less insipid, and in general a less disagreeable diet on future generations? It may be remembered that at one time the lancet was the panacea for all diseases. . . . Possibly the pap craze will go the way of the lancet."

WITH regard to viticulture in America we have to record this remarkable fact, that vines from Europe do not succeed in that country, and that long continued and often repeated experience shows, that to produce grapes and wine in America of any quality, recourse must be had to indigenous vines.

In California, European vines seem to grow, and bear fruit, but it lacks the essential quality of specificity; the wines made on the west coast have no flavour.

Viticulture has of late years not progressed much in America even on the Ohio, which was termed the Rhine of North America, and where there were some 1,550 acres of vineyards under cultivation. At St. Louis some very good effervescent wine was made and even brought to London.

In 1830 Prince counted more than eighty-eight varieties of American wild vines, but of these only a few were cultivated either for making wine or for eating as fruit. The vines were also described in a monograph by Durand, translated into French by M. des Moulins. In consequence of the ravages of the oidium and the phylloxera French viticulturists turned their attention to American vines, which were said not to be liable to the attacks of these vegetable animal parasites.

But no good wine could be obtained from any of them, and the only way of utilizing the immunity of their roots from the phylloxera was to graft European vines upon American stems.

In the Malayan towns and villages, although many dwellings are simply termed huts, these structures are nevertheless constructed with considerable care. To illustrate the style of building, Mr. Anderson's description of Jambi on the eastern coast provides a clear example: many houses are neatly sided and partitioned with planks and roofed with tiles of excellent manufacture. While a few homes feature thatched roofs or sides constructed from large, thick pieces of bark, the settlement also includes numerous houses built upon rafts made from huge tree trunks. These rafts allow the houses to float and move during the river's periodic swells, though in the dry season, they settle onto a sandy flat. Furthermore, smaller rafts support diminutive huts attached to the wealthier residences, which are used for bathing, an activity apparently favored by the women.

Regarding the inhabitants, the Malays generally adhere to the Mohammedan religion, yet their observance of its ordinances is not strict. Their governance is characterized by arbitrariness, as their sultans and chieftains operate without legal restraint and show little regard for humanitarian concerns.

Moving inland, the island is principally occupied by a distinct race that has historically maintained little contact with Europeans. This group resides in small villages, each governed by separate chiefs. These communities maintain their own systems of law, some codified, through which they punish offenders and resolve disputes. Notably, many members of these communities, especially the women, suffer from significant throat swellings, similar to the goitres found in the Alps.

A specific region, stretching across part of the country up to the bay of Tappa nooli, is home to the Battas people. These communities differ from the other Sumatran nations in their language, customs, and manner of life; critically, they possess no king and exist independently, with their various tribes often in conflict. To defend themselves, the Battas build their villages with formidable fortifications: double fences of pointed camphor plank, interspersed with fire-hardened, pointed bamboo pieces concealed by grass. Should enemies fall into their grasp, it is reported that they are executed and consumed, with their skulls hung up as trophies in the houses where unmarried men and boys reside and eat. Socially, they permit polygamy, allowing a man to acquire as many wives as he desires, though the number rarely surpasses eight. In their unpartitioned homes, all five wives typically share a single fire-place with the husband. This region is also the primary source of the cassia sent to Europe; the cassia-tree grows tall, reaching fifty or sixty feet, with a substantial two-foot-diameter stem and a beautiful, regularly spreading head.

In a separate location, BANCA, situated near the south-eastern part of Sumatra, spans approximately 95 miles in length and 30 miles in breadth. This area is renowned for its mines, which yield four million pounds of tin annually for the Dutch, thanks to the labor of Chinese colonists. Although the British held control over Banca for a period, they subsequently transferred it to the King of the Netherlands in exchange for territory on the Malabar coast.

Meanwhile, JAVA holds greater significance as the central locus of Dutch power within India than for its own general importance. This island stretches about 600 miles in length and 90 miles in breadth. Despite the poor health conditions in the maritime areas, the Dutch established the city of Batavia on its north-western coast in 1619. After a brief period of British control, they have maintained possession of Batavia to the present day. THE "Appeal to the Pulpit," which was some time ago sent by the Peace Society to 38,000 ministers in charge in the United Kingdom, was followed by this influentially signed letter, which was kindly prepared for the Secretary by the Rev. F. B. Meyer,

The undersigned, representing various Christian Communities, trust that they may be forgiven if they make a special appeal to the religious leaders of this nation, at the present crisis, to exert their great personal and public influence in the interests of Peace.

In the Far East a terrible war is in progress; and, although its theatre is on the other side of the globe, and it is generally agreed that the area of conflict should be restricted, there is no certainty that it may not suddenly and swiftly involve the Western nations also. So vast are the personal and national interests which are involved; so inflammable are racial passions and prejudices; so close is our connection by treaty with one of the combatants; that at any moment some episode of war may excite an alınost irresistible ebullition of feeling, and hurry our country to take part in the fray.

We are thankful to know that his Majesty the King has exerted his vast influence to secure a better understanding among European peoples, but there are still grave causes for apprehension that difficulties may arise in the settlement of Macedonia.

Under these circumstances the Christian pulpit has a very important part to play in allaying the passions of men, and directing their minds to the first principles of the Kingdom of God. A notable example of the effect of such remonstrance and appeal was given at the time of the Venezuela trouble with America, when the pulpits on both sides of the Atlantic rendered signal service in checking the spirit of war.

We therefore respectfully ask you to bring before your people, in your prayers and discourses, the Gospel of Peace of Our Lord and Master Jesus Christ, and to make use of any opportunity that may present itself of urging on your congregations to abstain, so far as may be possible, from any word or act which would be inconsistent with the spirit of the prayer, so specially appropriate at this time: "Give Peace in our Time, O Lord."
