A vote on the Arizona statehood bill was taken in the house territories committee this morning, despite the secrecy surrounding the meeting. The measure was ultimately defeated by a narrow margin of 5 to 6. The primary cause for this defeat was the objection that granting statehood would increase the number of free silver advocates in the senate; this concern was also linked to the sentiment regarding other bills that would similarly add six new free coinage men to the body.

Separately, in the house committee on elections No. B, Chairman McCall addressed the case of Hoge against Otey. Mr. Otey sought to reopen the case to present further evidence, claiming democratic notaries had refused to cooperate, and asked the committee to compel the necessary action.

Regarding Cuban recognition, the house foreign affairs committee is not expected to take action until the correspondence sent to the house yesterday has been printed and distributed to members. To ensure members fully grasp the situation in the island before a resolution on Cuban recognition is considered, Chairman Adams of the subcommittee is delaying the committee's next meeting until next week to allow for thorough review of the correspondence.

Shifting to the Behring Sea Question, yesterday afternoon, the treaty between the United States and Great Britain concerning alleged Behring sea fishery seizures was presented to the Senate and referred to the committee on foreign relations. This morning, the committee considered the convention, although no conclusion was reached because Senator Morgan spent considerable time elaborating on his views and their connection to the Paris arbitration court's findings.

This treaty, signed by Secretary of State Olney for the U.S. and Ambassador Pauncefote for Great Britain, outlines a process involving one commissioner from each government; if they fail to reach a conclusion, an umpire is to be selected, or if they cannot agree on an umpire, the President of the Swiss republic will name one. Whatever this commission agrees upon will be binding. However, the committee found the treaty text unsatisfactory because it addressed Great Britain's claims against the U.S. for alleged illegal seizures while ignoring potential claims by U.S. citizens against Canada or Great Britain. Therefore, an amendment will be made to correct this oversight.

This treaty itself is a direct result of the Paris tribunal's finding, which declined to rule on damages, leaving that question for the future. Following this, Great Britain claimed a specific amount, prompting legislative communication to the last congress urging the appropriation of $425,900 to cover these claims. The Senate, heavily influenced by Senator Morgan, subsequently refused to approve this appropriation, contending that passing such a bill would imply an admission that the Paris award included the subject of damages. This led to the conclusion that the only proper way to settle the question of damages was through a separate investigation, and the legality of the claims presented to the U.S. was denied. The convention now brings the matter before the Senate, which the committee deemed the proper procedure, and it is anticipated that a report favoring the treaty will follow soon after it is amended to equally protect U.S. rights alongside those of Great Britain.

Finally, in a separate legislative action, Mr. Gillett of Massachusetts introduced a bill in the house today designed to prevent state anti-gambling laws from being circumvented through interstate gambling via telegraph, telephone, or other means, extending the penalties for such activity to those provided for interstate gambling by mail.

Nine to ten o'clock was usually his hour for bed, while daylight in winter and shortly after in summer saw him in his stables or kennel.

He never betted, much less gambled. I don't think he knew a game with cards, and certainly he could not play billiards, and he hated smoking with intensity.

Briscoe had his fads and his faults, like other people; but, unlike others, he had no vices. He was not fond of imparting his knowledge to others, being very jealous of it, nor could he brook contradiction or opposition on subjects upon which he considered he was better informed than others. In fact, he was dictatorial in debate and determined in having his opinions adopted by others, and seldom would he adopt theirs. This propensity rendered him, as he certainly was, imperious in manner, although courteous and affable, but second fiddle he could play to no man.

Although many years my senior, we were always the greatest friends, and he told me a lot more about hunting than I think he ever did to anyone else. I had, however, to humour him, and at times to employ stratagems to get out of him what I wanted. No plan succeeded better than to make what I knew was a palpably wrong remark. Immediately my poor soul would be consigned to Avernus, and my body likened to a sanguinary donkey's, but I cared not for body or soul so long as I drew from old Henry the shapes which constituted the perfect foxhound or the weight-carrying hunter. This, through the means of my idiotic remarks, I generally did, either by descriptive dialogue, or, better still, by practical illustration on the flags of the kennels and in the stables.

For many years my Sundays were generally spent with him. When church was over I accompanied the family to Tinvane, and after an early dinner the remainder of the evening was spent among the hounds and horses. Under the apple-trees in the old orchard, "and the bustling pack at my feet," many a lesson was given me by him, and from such a mentor it was not difficult to learn something about the shapes of a foxhound and the theory of working him.

Never did I enjoy interviews with anyone more than I did those with my dear and genial friend, nor shall I ever do so again.

Since the now long-past period of these, my Sunday-school visits to Tinvane, I have seen a great many kennels, and a great many packs of foxhounds. I sball, therefore, put on paper what has occurred to me with regard to the construction of kennels in general and those for foxhounds in particular.

It strikes me that a lot of unnecessary trouble and expense is at times gone to in building kennels. Of course, as with most things, it is nicer to have them fitted smartly than otherwise; but I am pretty certain that expensive adornments are not necessary adjuncts to the well-being of a pack of hounds. Take, for instance, the old kennels at Tinvane. In them hounds enjoyed the very best of good health, and from them showed the very best of sport. Yet every detail, though perfect in its principle, was of the simplest description, and, like the Irishman's cabin, "with not a single thing for show." I know many others fitted up with all sorts of grandeur and even luxury for the hounds, but lamentably deficient in the all-important principle-sanitary arrangements-with the result that in them kennel lameress and other disorders are constantly to be found, while in the field the work of the occupants is by no means first-rate nor is good sport shown.

The great thing for kennels is to have them built upon stiff clay or rock, with a southern or south-western aspect, good drainage, with large and lofty lodging rooms. Ground damp must be prevented.

Water should be carefully looked to, for some sorts engender disease in hounds, and all sorts will cause rheumatism if conveyed any distance through leaden pipes. The flags must be of a quick-drying description.
